## 108. Decisions adopted and open after rev0013

Adopted:

- standard padded Base64 fields have one accepted textual spelling per octet string;
- all carried Base64 decoders enforce strict decode plus exact re-encode equality;
- non-zero pad bits, missing/excess padding, whitespace, and the wrong alphabet are rejected rather than normalized;
- native protocol integer fields require exact integer type and cannot inherit Python Boolean subtype semantics;
- WIRE-001 remains a named historical finding with public synthetic reproductions;
- malformed-input evidence is a distinct lane from deterministic known-answer review;
- the malformed corpus binds exact implementation sources and regenerates byte-for-byte;
- the actual native validators, actual carried worker RPC, and exact carried client functions execute the corpus;
- ordinary Chromium evidence remains separately scoped and honestly names navigation unavailability;
- the deterministic rev0012 vectors remain reproducible and carry explicit lineage rather than being silently rewritten;
- `impact`, `source`, `find`, `inspect`, `compare`, extract/build/repack, and no-clobber export remain available to the next officer;
- the constitution now has forty articles, including C40 on canonical wire spellings and exact types;
- the attributed handoff is `letter-0017-officer`;
- all thirteen exact donor records and all thirty-seven infrastructure candidates remain carried;
- research online every turn remains mandatory;
- unavailable, failed, interrupted, and passed remain different evidence states with no shame attached to unavailable tools or environments;
- delivery remains exactly three files.

Open:

- a bounded raw-JSON duplicate-name and interoperable-number boundary, only if its implementation is smaller and more reviewable than the ambiguity it removes;
- property-based and coverage-guided differential fuzzing with retained seeds, provenance, minimization rules, and explicit resource bounds;
- formal schemas for every signed application object and generated cross-provider conformance cases;
- Unicode and display-confusable policy for usernames, room labels, and fingerprint presentation without silently rewriting message text;
- independent review of the adapted TypeScript/JavaScript/WASM arithmetic and complete application protocol;
- constant-time and side-channel analysis in relevant browser and native environments;
- a designed room-session ratchet with offline, replay, membership-change, recovery, multi-device, and rollback semantics written before implementation;
- device-specific subkeys, device loss, device revocation, and profile merge governance;
- multi-owner rooms, owner transfer, moderation, membership convergence, and conflict resolution;
- a genuinely separate witness backend for a concrete managed-provider deployment;
- public provider operation, rate limits, abuse controls, billing, legal terms, and credential rotation;
- deployment-grade coturn, direct NAT traversal, automatic Linux hole punching, and Tor-aware local ergonomics;
- PQ protection below the application envelope or encrypted signaling metadata;
- voice/video, notifications, presence, accessibility expansion, and durable offline delivery.

The next recommended move is **not** to relax the new boundary for convenience. Choose between two bounded branches:

1. design a raw-JSON admission layer and prove through differential cases that it rejects duplicate names and unsafe number forms before host parsing can erase the evidence; or
2. write the room-ratchet state/recovery/membership memorandum as an inert carried design object, with no deployed ratchet until its offline and removal semantics are answerable.

Prefer the first only if the parser surface can remain small, dependency-free, and reviewable. Prefer the second if parser work would add more unreviewed code than it removes ambiguity. In either branch, preserve WIRE-001 and the rev0012 vector lineage. Do not turn a stricter protocol into a permissive “legacy mode” merely to make old malformed fixtures pass.

Preserve the current-first briefing, all historical receipts, the forty-article constitution, seventeen attributed letters, thirty-seven-source catalog, sixty-five technical-source records through T70, all thirty-seven infrastructure candidates, thirteen exact donor records, source/projection distinctions, public-vector credential prohibition, WIRE-001 corpus, no-clobber boundaries, no-fetch crypto rule, exact-type rule, and no-shame evidence discipline. Return one correctly named three-member ZIP and one link.

## 110. Rev0014 continuation record — Gatehouse begins before interpretation

Wireglass ended with a concrete choice. One branch was to stop at exact Base64 spellings and exact post-parse types, leaving the remaining raw-JSON ambiguity named. The other was to add a small admission layer only if that layer could be more reviewable than the ambiguity it removed. Gatehouse takes the second branch.

The reason is not that JSON is intrinsically unsuitable. The problem is the location of the first irreversible transformation. The application can validate a dictionary or JavaScript object after a host parser creates it, but by then several facts about the received text may be gone. Two decoded names may have become one property. An integer outside JavaScript’s exact range may have become a neighboring `Number`. Negative zero, a fraction, or exponent notation may have collapsed into a value whose later canonical spelling differs. Python and JavaScript may have accepted different extensions or represented the same token with different types. Once the original distinction is gone, a later schema check cannot honestly claim to have rejected it.

This matters because Vibechat uses JSON objects as more than display conveniences. Public cards, signed room policies, encrypted event headers, capability records, policy-adoption receipts, WebRTC signaling, managed TURN custody state, profiles, and relay records participate in hashes, signatures, recipient selection, replay decisions, and durable recovery. The cryptographic primitive may behave exactly while the application disagrees about the value that reached it. That is a protocol defect even when no signature is forged and no ciphertext is opened.

Gatehouse therefore adopts a temporal rule:

> Admit the original protocol bytes or text under one exact application language before a general host parser is allowed to erase distinctions relevant to the record.

This is not a claim that Vibechat has replaced every JSON implementation or built a universal standards parser. It is a deliberately small front gate. After the gate admits one value, the ordinary host representation and all existing message-specific validators still do their work. The new layer answers only whether the original record belongs to the language Vibechat has chosen to interpret at all.

The historical distinction remains important. WIRE-001 found permissive Base64 spelling and Python Boolean subtype behavior in rev0012 and repaired them in rev0013. WIRE-002 finds a prior-to-schema ambiguity still present in rev0013 and repairs it in rev0014. The findings are related but not merged. A future officer should be able to say which revision observed which defect, which exact sources were bound, and which fixtures demonstrate the repair.

## 111. The Gatehouse threat model

### 111.1 What the boundary protects

The boundary protects agreement about the value presented to application validation and cryptographic identity logic. Its immediate goals are:

- one decoded object name appears at most once in an object;
- a protocol integer has one canonical decimal spelling and one exact value in both Python and JavaScript;
- strings do not depend on lone-surrogate behavior or Unicode noncharacters that common interchange profiles warn against;
- one bounded JSON value consumes the complete admitted text;
- deeply nested structures do not receive an unbounded structural path merely because their byte count is small;
- byte-based ingresses reject malformed UTF-8 instead of replacing or silently interpreting it differently;
- every actual carried provider reaches the same decision for the retained corpus.

The boundary does not prove that an admitted message is authorized, signed, current, semantically reasonable, or safe to act upon. Admission precedes those checks. A unique member called `signature` may still contain a bad signature. A safe integer version may still be unsupported. A syntactically admitted room policy may still fail the owner signature, chain, epoch, expected-head, or membership rules. A valid encrypted envelope may still be a duplicate. A valid relay frame may still come from an untrusted sender. Gatehouse makes those later refusals more meaningful; it does not replace them.

### 111.2 What the boundary does not protect

The boundary is not:

- a complete implementation of every RFC 8259 JSON feature;
- a certificate of I-JSON or JCS conformance;
- a claim that every generic JSON document should use this subset;
- a Unicode confusable-defense policy for user-visible names;
- normalization of message text or labels;
- a memory-exhaustion proof for every host;
- a parser correctness proof;
- coverage-guided fuzzing;
- constant-time code;
- a replacement for size limits, schema checks, signature verification, AEAD authentication, replay checks, room membership, or recovery rules;
- an independent security audit.

The application intentionally rejects valid general JSON forms that it does not need on signed and hashed protocol surfaces. In particular, it rejects fractions and exponent notation instead of inventing cross-language decimal semantics. It rejects integer spellings outside the binary64 safe range instead of asking JavaScript to round them. It rejects negative zero instead of treating its later normalization as harmless. This is a protocol design choice, not a statement that those JSON forms are universally defective.

### 111.3 Attack and failure sketches

The retained corpus includes small examples because small examples reveal the boundary cleanly.

A duplicate-name record can be written as:

```json
{"epoch":1,"epoch":2}
```

or with an escape-equivalent name:

```json
{"epoch":1,"\u0065poch":2}
```

A host that keeps the later value exposes only `epoch = 2` to schema validation. Another implementation could keep the first value or report the duplicate. An application signature over a reserialized object no longer identifies the original competition between values.

An unsafe integer record can use:

```json
{"serial":9007199254740993}
```

Python preserves that integer. JavaScript’s `Number` cannot preserve it exactly. A signature generated by one provider over a canonicalized representation may therefore fail elsewhere, or worse, two distinct texts may be treated as one numeric value in one provider while remaining distinct in another.

Negative zero exposes a lexical/value distinction:

```json
{"serial":-0}
```

JavaScript can temporarily represent negative zero, but ordinary stringification emits `0`. An application that accepts the input and later hashes its normalized output has silently changed the spelling it claims to identify.

A fractional or exponent form can do the same:

```json
{"serial":1.0}
{"serial":1e0}
```

Both become the number `1` in JavaScript. The project needs no fractional protocol fields, so refusing the forms is simpler than specifying their canonical semantic path.

A lone surrogate string such as `"\ud800"` is accepted by some host parsers into a language-specific string value that is not a Unicode scalar sequence. Later UTF-8 encoding behavior, display, comparison, and serialization can differ. Gatehouse rejects it before application data is constructed.

None of these examples is presented as a complete exploit against the prior revision. They establish that the old admission claim was too broad. The repaired claim is narrower and testable: the named raw texts are either admitted with an exact canonical value or rejected before schema validation.

## 112. The admitted language and its implementation

### 112.1 Exact bytes and UTF-8

Where an ingress begins as bytes, the byte limit is checked before decoding and UTF-8 decoding is strict. Browser file reads use a fatal `TextDecoder`; native files and network records use strict UTF-8 decoding. The byte-order mark is not accepted as invisible protocol decoration. The parser consumes one value and then requires end of input apart from JSON whitespace. Trailing values or arbitrary suffix text are rejected.

Existing ingress bounds remain. Gatehouse does not replace a 64 KiB bridge-body limit, a relay-frame limit, a profile limit, a file-record limit, or a provider-response limit with one universal number. The correct sequence is: enforce the caller’s byte custody rule, decode exactly, admit the structure, then apply the message-specific schema and cryptographic checks.

### 112.2 Object members

Object-member names are compared after JSON escape processing. This is essential. A byte-level search for repeated quoted substrings would miss `"room"` versus `"r\u006fom"`. The native parser uses Python’s `object_pairs_hook`, which receives the ordered member pairs before they become a dictionary. It validates each decoded key and refuses a key already present in the current object.

JavaScript’s `JSON.parse` offers no equivalent duplicate callback. The carried worker and client therefore use a small recursive-descent admission reader. It recognizes the selected JSON grammar, decodes strings, records each decoded name in a set for its object, and rejects a repeat before returning the value. Only after this pass does the application use the ordinary resulting value and the existing validators.

Uniqueness is local to each object, as JSON object scope requires. The same name may appear in distinct nested objects. The rule concerns competing members in one object, not global field-name uniqueness across a document.

### 112.3 Strings

Admitted strings are sequences of Unicode scalar values. An escaped high surrogate must be followed by a valid escaped low surrogate and the pair becomes one supplementary scalar. An unpaired high or low surrogate is refused. Literal control characters remain invalid under the JSON grammar. Unicode noncharacters are refused according to the chosen interchange boundary.

The parser does **not** normalize ordinary valid strings. The exact message text is not silently changed from one normalization form to another. Username normalization remains its own explicitly documented account rule. Room display labels remain subject to their own field limits. A future confusable-display policy must not be smuggled into this parser by rewriting content.

### 112.4 Numbers

Gatehouse accepts protocol numbers only when they match this conceptual grammar:

```text
0
-?[1-9][0-9]*
```

The value must fall within:

```text
-9007199254740991 .. 9007199254740991
```

`-0` is refused. Leading zeros are refused by the JSON grammar and the canonical-integer check. A decimal point, exponent, `NaN`, positive infinity, and negative infinity are refused. The host representation after admission is an exact integer on both sides of the native/worker boundary.

This is stricter than many current field schemas. It is useful precisely because a new field cannot accidentally acquire cross-provider floating-point semantics merely because its author remembered to check only `typeof value === "number"`. Field validators still check ranges such as version `=== 1`, nonnegative milliseconds, epoch progression, bounded fragment counts, and serial relationships.

### 112.5 Depth

The maximum admitted nesting depth is sixty-four arrays or objects. The retained cases include an accepted value at the limit and a rejected value beyond it. Depth is counted structurally, not inferred from a byte heuristic. The native path walks the admitted value after parsing; the worker/client readers track depth during descent.

A depth limit is one resource control, not a complete complexity theorem. Large member counts, long strings, cryptographic work, attachment chunking, relay quotas, and browser storage remain independently bounded. Future fuzzing should keep wall-clock and allocation ceilings explicit.

### 112.6 One boundary, three provider forms

The native, worker, and client implementations are intentionally similar in policy but suited to their hosts:

- `native.py` uses standard-library decoder hooks to preserve member pairs and raw numeric tokens, then validates strings and depth.
- `worker.ts` carries a recursive admission reader in the embedded secret-holding worker and exposes a review-only `json-admit` RPC that holds no identity state.
- `client.js` carries the matching browser/application reader and uses fatal UTF-8 file decoding before imports. Its exact admission function can also be executed under Node for a separate deterministic lane.

The three implementations are not claimed to be formally equivalent. Their retained agreement is evidence for named cases. The source bindings make later changes visible. If one implementation changes, the relevant impact map includes admission, malformed-input, interoperability, browser, WebRTC, and carrier review rather than pretending a matching function name preserved evidence automatically.

## 113. Ingress inventory and custody order

The most important implementation work was not adding the parser functions. It was following untrusted text to the places where the old host parser ran first.

### 113.1 Encrypted content

AEAD authentication answers whether ciphertext and associated data match a key. It does not choose a JSON language. Decrypted event payloads now pass raw-text admission before event-type validation. This includes ordinary chat, file metadata/chunks, room-policy courier records, capability queries/responses, and policy-adoption receipts. Control records remain distinguished from ordinary chat after admission.

The content boundary therefore reads:

```text
ciphertext bytes
  -> AEAD authentication/decryption
  -> strict UTF-8
  -> raw JSON admission
  -> exact event schema/type checks
  -> signature/domain/room/epoch/replay logic
  -> application state or rendering
```

No stage is described as proving the next one.

### 113.2 Public cards and policies

Public cards and room-policy files are public metadata, but they are still untrusted inputs. A card now passes raw admission before Base64 canonicality, key lengths, suite, version, fingerprint recomputation, and explicit user pin confirmation. A room policy passes admission before canonical-body identity, owner signature, chain, epoch, expected previous head, membership bounds, and local disposition rules.

This ordering matters for the old WIRE-001 fixtures. The same-key noncanonical Base64 card remains rejected by the later Base64 boundary. Gatehouse does not erase that evidence by making the raw JSON gate responsible for every malformed field.

### 113.3 Profiles and stored records

Encrypted profiles are authenticated before their plaintext enters the raw parser. Imported profile envelopes and stored record files also pass exact byte/text admission before their own envelope and merge rules. An older authenticated profile still cannot erase newer invitation decisions, pending policy knowledge, capability state, adoption receipts, or room heads already held locally.

Browser persistence keeps its ordering rule: application state is written successfully before ciphertext acceptance activates the duplicate shortcut. IndexedDB promises wait for transaction completion, not only request success. Gatehouse adds parsing discipline without weakening write/receipt discipline.

### 113.4 Relay, federation, and terminal frames

WebSocket and native TCP relay frames, federation frames, readiness messages, terminal relay input, and public input files pass admission before frame-type and token/custody checks. The blind relay remains blind to message plaintext and identity secrets. Gatehouse does not turn a well-shaped frame into authorization to retain arbitrary data; quotas, tokens, record shape, and endpoint verification remain separate.

The development test driver now separates `cli` from `transport`. The CLI lane owns native cryptographic/state-machine assertions. The transport lane owns actual WebSocket/TCP/federation/restart/PTY/courier movement. This avoids one long orchestration obscuring which boundary is still running and gives interrupted work a more useful partial receipt.

### 113.5 WebRTC and managed infrastructure

Signed WebRTC signal packets, fragment records, and reassembled data-channel frames pass admission before signaling schema, sender/recipient, session/reply relationship, signature, and data-channel handling. SDP remains authenticated but not application-encrypted. Chat/file/control content remains independently PQ-encrypted before fragmentation.

Managed TURN API responses, encrypted journal plaintext, external witness/provider responses, and native bridge request bodies also use the boundary. Provider API tokens, journal keys, witness keys, TURN passwords, and ICE credential fields remain excluded from the public carrier and evidence objects. A strictly parsed response is not proof that a public provider performed the operation; local shaped fixtures remain local shaped fixtures.

### 113.6 Trusted carried data remains named separately

The embedded constitution, letters, research catalog, lineage ledger, evidence ledger, source manifest, and compile-time vendor records are exact manifest-bound source in the carrier. They are not reclassified as hostile network records solely to claim more parser coverage. Local presentation preferences likewise remain presentation data.

This is an important review habit: grep findings start an inquiry; they do not settle the trust boundary. Every new `JSON.parse` or `json.loads` call should be accompanied by an answer to “which bytes can reach this call, and what evidence would be lost here?”

## 114. WIRE-002 as a carried review object

### 114.1 Corpus identity

The new source members are:

```text
vibe-admission-corpus  -> protocol_json.json
vibe-admission-tests   -> protocol_json_checks.py
```

The finding identity is:

```text
WIRE-002-raw-json-admission-before-host-parse
```

The corpus contains twenty-seven public synthetic cases. Six are accepted and twenty-one are rejected. The accepted group demonstrates empty/ordinary objects, escape-decoded unique names, safe integer extrema, a supplementary Unicode scalar, arrays containing Boolean/null/integer values, and the maximum admitted nesting depth. The rejected group covers plain and escape-equivalent duplicates, unsafe integers, negative zero, fractions, exponents, malformed or problematic string cases, excessive nesting, a leading byte-order mark, and trailing data.

The packet also preserves host differentials. Those examples deliberately show what a default host parser does **before** the application gate: duplicate names disappear, JavaScript rounds an unsafe integer, negative zero or decimal spelling normalizes, and Python/JavaScript expose different numeric behavior. The differential records are explanations and regressions, not instructions to accept the default behavior.

### 114.2 Regeneration and source binding

`protocol_json_checks.py` regenerates the packet from its exact sources and compares bytes. The packet binds:

```text
native.py
worker.ts
worker.js
client.js
dev.py
```

The first four implement or execute admission. `dev.py` carries the workshop command and source catalog that exports and explains the packet. A matching packet identity says these exact sources produced this exact review object. It does not independently bless the code.

The officer commands are:

```bash
bash Vibechat.html admission
bash Vibechat.html admission --full
bash Vibechat.html admission --output new-protocol-json.json
bash Vibechat.html impact vibe-admission-corpus
bash Vibechat.html impact vibe-admission-tests
bash test.sh --html Vibechat.html --output new-admission-receipt admission
```

Output paths must be absent. Exported review packets are public synthetic material. They are not credentials and do not authorize protocol traffic.

### 114.3 Executed surfaces

The admission lane executes:

1. the actual native raw-text helper;
2. the actual embedded worker through its carried review-only RPC;
3. the exact carried client admission function under Node;
4. the corpus generator and source-binding checks;
5. selected default-host-parser differential witnesses.

Each accepted case must be admitted consistently and produce the expected canonical value. Each rejected case must be refused by all three actual providers. The lane records ninety-two scoped assertions. The count overlaps source-binding, regeneration, case, and boundary assertions and is not a security score.

Ordinary Chromium workflows remain a separate lane. That lane crosses browser file APIs, product UI, the carried worker, storage collaborators, room operations, managed-provider controls, restart custody, and the no-external-fetch boundary. The admission lane does not borrow those claims merely because it executes client code under Node.

### 114.4 Retained WIRE-001 and vector lineage

The malformed-input packet from rev0013 remains carried. Its forty-five assertions still exercise canonical padded Base64, nonzero pad bits, missing/excess padding, whitespace, wrong alphabet, same-key alternate card text, Boolean version fields, and provider agreement. WIRE-002 does not change its `fixed_in` revision or rebrand its cases.

The deterministic protocol-review packet also remains carried. Its seeds and vector messages remain rooted in rev0012. Rev0014 refreshes exact source bindings because the worker/native sources changed at the admission boundary. The vector lineage states this explicitly. Reproducible vectors are not silently regenerated and presented as if their provenance began today.

## 115. Online research performed in the Gatehouse turn

Research was performed online again before editing and is recorded in `research.json`. All thirty-seven previously investigated infrastructure candidates remain present with their earlier review histories; this turn did not pretend that a parser review refreshed provider pricing, quotas, terms, or availability.

### 115.1 RFC 8259 — JSON syntax and interoperability warnings

RFC 8259 defines the JSON grammar and explains that object names should be unique for interoperable behavior. It also notes that software behavior is unpredictable when names repeat. Its number grammar permits fractions and exponents, while its interoperability discussion identifies the common exact-integer range associated with IEEE 754 binary64 implementations.

Vibechat uses the source to separate general JSON from an application protocol profile. The RFC does not require every application to reject every fraction or exponent. Gatehouse rejects them because the project has no fractional protocol fields and because retaining them would require a more complex cross-provider canonical-number contract.

### 115.2 RFC 7493 — I-JSON

The retained I-JSON review was revisited. I-JSON requires UTF-8, forbids duplicate object names, restricts interoperable numbers, and addresses Unicode string interoperability. Those constraints strongly support checking raw input before a host representation erases duplicate or numeric evidence.

Gatehouse deliberately avoids claiming complete I-JSON certification. It implements a narrower number profile and its own explicit string/noncharacter rule. The retained corpus is finite, and no standards body examined this implementation.

### 115.3 ECMAScript `JSON.parse`

The current ECMAScript algorithm was reviewed for duplicate-name and number behavior. Later duplicate names take precedence in the resulting object, and JSON numeric text becomes JavaScript `Number` values. That behavior is useful and specified for the host language; it simply does not preserve the evidence Gatehouse needs before application admission.

The project therefore does not wrap `JSON.parse` and claim duplicate detection afterwards. The worker/client readers observe the raw text first. Ordinary `JSON.parse` remains appropriate after admission and for trusted local records where no protocol claim depends on the lost syntax.

### 115.4 Python standard-library `json`

Python’s decoder provides `object_pairs_hook`, `parse_int`, `parse_float`, and `parse_constant`. Gatehouse uses those hooks to refuse duplicate decoded names, inspect integer tokens before conversion, reject fractions/exponents, and reject non-finite extensions. The resulting structure is then walked for depth and scalar-string rules.

The Python documentation also makes the default behavior relevant: repeated names ordinarily leave the last value, and non-finite constants can be accepted. The review does not condemn the general-purpose library. It uses the library’s intended extension points to define a stricter application language.

### 115.5 Research discipline

No standards text was treated as proof of security. The exact research claim is that the sources informed the chosen boundary and the negative fixtures. They do not establish parser correctness, side-channel resistance, protocol soundness, provider interoperability beyond the executed cases, or independent review.

Research online every turn remains constitutional. Future research records should distinguish the publication date, review date, exact design question, and what the source did not establish. Fast-changing provider facts must be rechecked when a turn relies on them; carrying an old URL is not a current verification.

## 116. Workshop machinery and officer ergonomics

### 116.1 Thirty-nine named source members

Gatehouse carries thirty-nine named source members. The two additions are the WIRE-002 corpus and its executable checks. The source inventory remains available without extraction:

```bash
bash Vibechat.html inspect
bash Vibechat.html source vibe-admission-corpus --start 1 --lines 120
bash Vibechat.html source vibe-admission-tests --start 1 --lines 160
bash Vibechat.html find strict_json --limit 20
bash Vibechat.html impact vibe-worker-source
```

`source` is line-bounded. `find` is literal and result-bounded. `impact` is a declared review map, not inferred dependency completeness. `inspect` reports identities and sizes; it does not grant execution permission.

### 116.2 Separate CLI and transport lanes

The officer driver now exposes:

```text
cli
transport
browser
provider
journal
witness
webrtc
interop
review
malformed
admission
carrier
all
bench
```

The CLI lane owns native self-tests, credential logic, room state, courier state, decline/reconsider recovery, adoption receipts, and capability discovery. The transport lane owns actual endpoint/relay movement, federation, restart, a Bash/PTY terminal exercise, and encrypted courier delivery across WebSocket and TCP.

This split was made after one aggregate run exceeded its outer execution window while completed sub-suites were still passing. The partial checkpoint was retained as partial and not promoted. Separating the lanes makes future ownership clearer and preserves useful receipts without calling interruption a product failure or a pass.

### 116.3 Raw-response fixture repair

The new product client reads native bridge responses as raw text and applies Gatehouse before it interprets the JSON. Several browser development fixtures still returned mock objects exposing only a `.json()` method. That fixture shape bypassed the newly required raw-response boundary and caused the workspace to remain locked with `response.text is not a function`.

The repair was to make the explicit native-RPC collaborators return a response-shaped object with `.text()` over `JSON.stringify(body)` as well as the older `.json()` helper. The product client was not weakened to accommodate the fixture. Browser, WebRTC, and DOM adapters were updated together. This is an example of a good test failure: the production boundary changed, and the mock had to become more faithful rather than teaching production code to accept a second path.

Future officers should preserve this rule. A fixture that hands an already decoded object to code meant to test raw admission has skipped the subject of the test. The fixture may still be useful for later schema/state checks, but its scope must be named honestly.

### 116.4 Checkpointed receipt behavior

`test.sh --output ABSENT_DIR ...` writes a partial report during execution and a final report only when the lane terminates. It never overwrites an existing output directory. Completed suite artifacts can remain useful after interruption, but `test-report.partial.json` is not renamed or described as complete.

Every final report records the exact carrier path and SHA-256, revision, lane status, elapsed time, commands, exit codes, and captured standard output. Separate lane reports can therefore be compared without adding their assertion counts into one trust number.

### 116.5 Extract, build, repack, and compare

The carrier retains Lumen’s inspect-before-run and fresh-directory discipline and Hyperepo’s refusal to merge uncertain restoration into an existing workspace.

```bash
bash Vibechat.html extract --directory absent-workshop
bash Vibechat.html build --directory absent-workshop
bash Vibechat.html repack --directory absent-workshop --output absent-repacked.html
bash absent-repacked.html verify
```

Extraction and repack refuse overwrite by default. A fresh explicit TypeScript/WASM build uses carried readable sources and the available local compilers; it does not install packages or fetch modules. `compare` supports known carrier schemas through rev0014 and compares bytes without executing the target.

The development workspace is not the user-facing distribution shape. The delivery remains exactly three root files. Screenshots, logs, receipt directories, caches, compiler outputs, runtime databases, keys, provider tokens, and extracted trees stay outside the ZIP.

## 117. Constitution, letters, lineage, and donor machinery

The constitution now contains forty-one articles. C41 states the raw-text-before-host-interpretation rule, the exact admitted subset, the absence of a permissive legacy mode, and the limited meaning of a passing corpus. C40 remains the Base64/exact-type rule. Neither supersedes the broader articles on source/projection distinction, no-shame evidence, no hidden dependency fetching, private-state boundaries, room membership, provider custody, or publication authority.

The attributed handoff is `letter-0018-officer`. It records why the first branch was selected, what WIRE-002 found, where the parser was installed, which evidence was executed, what research was reviewed, and why the next recommendation shifts away from another parser feature. The earlier seventeen letters remain exact history rather than being rewritten to sound prescient.

`lineage.json` now records a rev0014 adaptation while preserving both donor inputs and all thirteen exact selected donor records. Gatehouse continues to borrow these forms rather than their branding:

- Lumen’s arrival guide: inspect the carrier, distinguish hashes from authority, and keep editable source separate from generated projection.
- Source Glass: let a future officer inspect exact carried source rather than a paraphrase of it.
- Change Radius: name the review obligations of a change without pretending the map is complete.
- Capsule Cutaway: show where the one-file carrier’s bytes live.
- Carrier Clinic: verify a copy locally without converting internal consistency into external trust.
- Hyperepo recovery: restore into an absent location, preserve uncertainty, and never treat recovered task text as fresh authority.
- Hyperepo bounded source catalog: retain exact records with identities and selection boundaries instead of carrying an unreviewed universe.

The sandpeople arrival guide remains at the top of the HTML. Conversations and constitutions remain available through the document. The code does not erase the prose that explains why it exists.

## 118. Decisions adopted and open after rev0014

Adopted:

- untrusted protocol JSON is admitted before ordinary host parsing can erase duplicate-name, number-spelling, or string evidence;
- byte ingresses use strict/fatal UTF-8 and retain their caller-specific size limits;
- decoded object-member names must be unique at every object level, including escape-equivalent names;
- admitted strings are Unicode scalar sequences and exclude Unicode noncharacters;
- admitted numbers are canonical base-ten safe integers only;
- negative zero, fractions, exponents, non-finite extensions, unsafe integers, excessive nesting, leading BOM, and trailing data are refused;
- there is no permissive legacy path for ambiguous protocol records;
- native, worker, and client carry matching policy implementations suited to their hosts;
- decrypted events, profiles, files, relay/federation frames, WebRTC signals/fragments, bridge bodies, managed-provider responses, journals, and witness/provider objects cross the gate before their schemas;
- WIRE-002 is retained as a public synthetic corpus with exact source bindings and actual provider execution;
- WIRE-001 remains separately named and fixed in rev0013;
- deterministic vector seeds/messages retain rev0012 lineage while source bindings advance;
- browser/DOM/WebRTC native-RPC fixtures now expose raw `.text()` responses so they exercise the production admission path;
- CLI/native and owned-loopback transport are separate officer lanes;
- the HTML carries thirty-nine named source members;
- the constitution has forty-one articles and the attributed handoff is `letter-0018-officer`;
- the research catalog has sixty-eight technical records through T73, all thirty-seven infrastructure candidates, and a rev0014 turn note;
- every turn continues to research online;
- unavailable, interrupted, failed, and passed remain distinct and carry no shame;
- the delivery remains exactly the canonical trio.

Open:

- property-based and coverage-guided differential fuzzing with retained seeds, exact source/tool provenance, minimization, time/memory ceilings, and corpus promotion rules;
- a formally documented schema for every signed or hashed application object;
- an explicit Unicode/display-confusable policy for usernames, labels, and fingerprint presentation that does not rewrite message content;
- independent review of the adapted TypeScript/JavaScript/WASM cryptographic implementation and application protocol;
- constant-time and side-channel analysis for native and browser environments;
- a designed room-session ratchet covering offline delivery, replay, removal, recovery, multi-device state, rollback, and post-compromise behavior before any deployed ratchet code;
- device-specific subkeys, loss/revocation, profile merge, and custody governance;
- multi-owner rooms, owner transfer, moderation, policy conflict resolution, and membership convergence;
- a genuinely separate external witness trust domain for one concrete managed-provider deployment;
- current public provider operation, abuse controls, quotas, billing, legal terms, token rotation, and reachability evidence;
- deployment-grade coturn, direct NAT traversal, automatic Linux hole punching, and Tor-aware local ergonomics;
- protection against WebRTC/signaling metadata and PQ protection below the application envelope;
- voice/video, presence, notifications, accessibility expansion, and durable offline delivery.

The recommended next move is now the **inert room-ratchet state memorandum**, not immediate ratchet code. Gatehouse has made the input language small enough to review; the highest product-security gap remains message-key evolution and recovery semantics. The memorandum should answer, before implementation:

1. Which state is per identity, device, room, sender, and membership epoch?
2. What does an offline member need to decrypt retained messages without allowing a removed member to decrypt future messages?
3. Which events advance a sending chain and which receipts are required before deletion of old key material?
4. How are out-of-order, duplicate, missing, and retransmitted messages handled?
5. What exact state must encrypted profiles retain, and what older-profile imports are refused?
6. How does a device join, leave, become lost, or become revoked?
7. What claim of forward secrecy or post-compromise security is actually supported under the chosen design?
8. How does room-policy epoch change interact with the ratchet, queued ciphertext, and policy-adoption receipts?
9. What deterministic public vectors and malformed-state cases are needed before a browser/native implementation exists?
10. Which secrets must never enter the carrier, logs, relay records, test corpus, screenshots, or bootstrap prose?

Keep that object inert and source-bound until the answers are coherent. Do not label ordinary per-message ML-KEM wrapping a ratchet, and do not borrow a protocol name without implementing its state and security properties. Parser expansion is not the next priority unless a concrete new cross-provider ambiguity is first demonstrated.

## 121. Wayglass design memorandum — why the first ratchet revision is deliberately inert

A project can make a dangerous mistake by implementing the part of a cryptographic protocol that is easiest to draw and postponing the state machine that determines whether it is safe to operate. A KDF chain is compact. Crash recovery, duplicate delivery, membership changes, concurrent devices, retries, profile restore, skipped keys and rollback are where the product decides whether that chain is used once, twice, or after it should have been retired.

Rev0015 therefore treats the state memorandum itself as a deliverable. It is machine-readable, source-bound, carried in the HTML, visible through the browser workshop and CLI, and exercised by a dedicated lane. The design is not hidden in this prose alone. `ratchet_memorandum.json` has format `vibechat-room-ratchet-memorandum-v1`, an explicit `inert-design-only` status, a body digest, exact source bindings and a fixed reference clock. Its recommended decision identity is:

```text
RR-001-pairwise-device-ratchet-fanout
```

The object says `recommended-implementation-target-not-authorization-to-code`. That phrase is operational. A later patch cannot cite RR-001 as permission to invent a KDF, choose unauthenticated prekeys, or claim forward secrecy. It must satisfy the implementation gates or create a new reviewed decision that explains why the gates changed.

### 121.1 Sixteen invariants

The memorandum carries sixteen normative invariants. In prose, their core is:

1. A room-policy epoch and a cryptographic ratchet epoch are different state.
2. Every pairwise session binds exact local and remote device lineages and an exact construction version.
3. One logical room event has one immutable identity even when it has multiple recipient envelopes.
4. Every recipient envelope binds the exact logical event, room policy, recipient device and session position.
5. A send advances on a clone and settles next state plus immutable outbox before emission.
6. A retry emits the already-settled envelope and never derives another message key.
7. A receive advances on a clone and settles next state plus deduplication before plaintext visibility.
8. Authentication, parse, bound or persistence failure discards candidate receive state.
9. Skipped-key derivation and storage are finite and explicitly bounded.
10. A removed or unauthorized device receives no newly created envelope.
11. A newly authorized device does not receive history automatically.
12. Policy adoption cannot manufacture a pairwise session.
13. Delivery, relay retention, recipient decryption and recipient application remain separate receipts.
14. Recovery profiles preserve one committed lineage; divergent secret state is not merged.
15. Complete state loss creates a new device/session lineage.
16. Local state cannot support unconditional rollback claims without an external monotonic anchor.

The exact wording and identifiers live in the JSON source. The summary above helps a reader, but tests bind the exact object rather than this paraphrase.

### 121.2 The logical-event manifest

A room message should not be defined by one particular recipient ciphertext. Its authored identity should be stable while transport and per-device encryption vary. The future logical-event manifest therefore needs, at minimum, the author identity/device, room identifier, exact accepted policy head, content type, content digest, creation nonce/identity and any reply/file relationships that are part of the authored message. It is signed once under a domain that cannot be confused with a room policy, WebRTC signal, prekey bundle, adoption receipt or recipient envelope.

Each recipient envelope then binds that logical-event identity plus recipient device and session header. This separation has several advantages:

* A retransmission can be proven to be the same recipient envelope rather than a newly authored event.
* A room timeline can deduplicate recipient copies without assuming ciphertext equality.
* A sender can report which recipients were offered an envelope without claiming they decrypted it.
* A relay can retain opaque recipient envelopes without learning plaintext or becoming the event author.
* A future authorized history export can retain the logical event and explicitly state which recipient envelopes or plaintext records it includes.

It also creates obligations. The manifest must not list a recipient device excluded by the exact policy. Envelope creation must not mutate the manifest. The event cannot be marked completely sent merely because one envelope settled. The UI must avoid presenting partial fanout as room-wide delivery unless the user explicitly accepted that mode.

### 121.3 Send settlement in more detail

A safe send transaction is conceptually:

```text
load exact room policy and recipient-device set
load one eligible session per recipient device
construct and sign one immutable logical-event manifest
for each required recipient session:
    clone committed send state
    derive candidate next chain state and one message key
    encrypt one recipient envelope bound to event/policy/device/session position
validate every candidate envelope and required recipient set
atomically write:
    all next committed send states
    immutable event manifest
    immutable recipient envelope bytes
    outbox settlement records
commit
only after commit, permit transport emission
```

This pseudocode does not select a cryptographic construction. It states the product ordering. If any required session cannot create a valid candidate, the default design aborts before committing any of the group of recipient transactions. Whether a later UI can authorize partial fanout remains open. It must never happen accidentally because one loop iteration failed after earlier envelopes were emitted.

A process crash after commit but before emission leaves a retryable outbox. A crash after some emissions leaves exact settled bytes to replay. A crash before commit leaves no permissible envelope to emit. An uncertain transport result changes delivery status, not key state or event identity.

### 121.4 Receive settlement in more detail

A safe receive transaction is conceptually:

```text
admit raw record before host parsing
validate exact schema and domain
locate exact sender-device/session lineage
check room policy authorization for the logical event
clone committed receive state
if needed, derive no more than MAX_SKIP skipped keys
authenticate and decrypt on the clone
validate event manifest, recipient binding and deduplication identity
atomically write:
    next receive state
    consumed/skipped-key changes
    deduplication result
    encrypted retained event/ciphertext custody as configured
commit
only after commit, surface plaintext or application/adoption receipt
```

The UI may show a rejected or quarantined record, but it must not show authenticated plaintext while persistence failed and then silently accept the same envelope again after restart. If the application chooses memory-only operation, that limitation must be visible and the security claim narrowed accordingly.

A skipped message key is not a general archive key. It is tied to one exact session position, stored under finite count/age limits, and deleted after successful use. The project cannot prove low-level secure erasure in JavaScript, Python, a browser profile, swap, filesystem snapshots or storage hardware. The construction may be designed for deletion, while the product claim remains bounded by the actual platform.

## 122. Device identity and asynchronous initialization are the next cryptographic gate

Pairwise ratcheting is not useful until two devices can initialize the right session while one is offline. That is not merely “run ML-KEM once.” A prekey bundle must say who authorized the device, which key is one-time or reusable, which algorithm/version/domain applies, when it expires, how reuse is detected, which server/peer may distribute it, and what the initiator must bind into the initial transcript.

Vibechat’s current identities are Argon2id-derived and expose ML-KEM and ML-DSA public material. The first ratchet implementation should not automatically reuse those long-lived private keys as every device’s prekey, signing key, ratchet secret and recovery key. The design needs a device authorization object signed by the user identity—or another equally explicit authorization chain—and separately generated device/prekey material. The user fingerprint and device fingerprint must both be visible where the distinction matters.

PQXDH is useful research because it handles an offline recipient and one-time post-quantum prekeys. It is not copied unchanged here. Its current revision explicitly relies on classical discrete-log assumptions for mutual authentication. Vibechat’s requirement is post-quantum authentication, so an adaptation using ML-DSA device authorization/prekey signatures needs an exact transcript, domain separation, replay story and review of what deniability or non-repudiation properties change. “Replace XEdDSA with ML-DSA” is not a complete protocol argument.

A bounded next design revision could therefore focus on an inert device authorization and prekey bundle format, with public synthetic vectors and one-time-use/replenishment state. That would still not authorize the ratchet implementation until the selected two-party construction and storage transactions are joined to it.

## 123. MLS remains a comparison and scaling path

RFC 9420 and RFC 9750 are not decorative citations. They demonstrate how much group state a mature design names: clients as cryptographic members, KeyPackages, credentials, Proposals, Commits, Welcome messages, epoch ordering, fresh entropy after membership change, per-epoch secret trees, application access control, delivery-service disorder and state-loss recovery.

Vibechat’s room policy already has an owner-signed linear membership history. That is not MLS. It lacks an MLS ratchet tree, key schedule, transcript, Commit/Welcome semantics and conformance behavior. The pairwise recommendation intentionally keeps that policy as application authorization while each device link evolves separately.

The active post-quantum MLS ciphersuite draft is important because PQC cannot be added to MLS by naming ML-KEM alone. Cipher-suite choices include KEM, signature, AEAD, hash and KDF implications, and some proposed suites provide post-quantum confidentiality with classical authentication while others add post-quantum signatures. The draft remains work in progress. A future MLS migration should use a reviewed implementation and then prove how Vibechat identities, room ownership, retained ciphertext custody, federation and history map into the application around MLS.

The expired amortized combiner draft remains useful as a warning against pretending performance tradeoffs are trivial. Post-quantum key material is larger; full updates, partial updates and freshness frequency affect bandwidth and recovery time. Its expired status is part of the record, so it is not treated as a selected standard.

## 124. Donor machinery taken again, without copying unrelated product claims

The second and third readings of Lumen and Hyperepo continue to pay off.

From **Lumen**, rev0015 keeps:

* an arrival guide before executable or opaque material;
* exact named source blocks and bounded source reading;
* Source Glass’s distinction between authored source and generated projection;
* Change Radius’s idea that a change should expose review obligations, not just a diff;
* Carrier Clinic’s local byte-identity checks without promoting hashes to trust;
* fresh-directory extraction and no recursive carrier embedding;
* the rule that a generated receipt is a claim about a bounded transformation, not truth or authority.

The ratchet memorandum benefits especially from Change Radius. It names what future code would disturb: identity cards, room policies, profile format, outbox, deduplication, relay retention, receipts, browser worker state, native storage and migration. A future officer can ask `impact vibe-ratchet-memorandum` and see the relevant test lane before editing.

From **Hyperepo**, rev0015 keeps:

* current-first guidance without deleting historical decisions;
* explicit distinction between active work, parked work and a recovered stale instruction;
* no-clobber outputs and state settlement before claiming completion;
* recovery into an absent destination rather than in-place merge;
* evidence states that distinguish passed, failed, unavailable and not attempted;
* the constitutional rule that missing tools or environments carry no shame and do not justify invented results.

That last rule matters for security work. We do not claim a rollback anchor because none was deployed. We do not call that a moral failure. We record the missing evidence and design the boundary so a later officer knows what would be required.

Neither donor supplies a ratchet protocol. Their contribution is machinery for carrying, inspecting, testing and honestly delimiting one.

## 125. The ratchet test object

`ratchet_checks.py` is intentionally a model checker for the memorandum’s public transition cases, not a cryptographic test. The current source report contains sixty-seven assertions before carrier command checks.

The twenty-eight transition cases include:

* first settled send;
* retry of the same outbox envelope;
* crash before send commit;
* crash after send commit and before emission;
* receive success and receive persistence failure;
* authentication failure without state advance;
* bounded out-of-order acceptance;
* skipped-key overflow refusal;
* duplicate envelope handling;
* room-policy removal before send;
* policy change while an older outbox exists;
* newly added device without a session;
* new session after explicit device authorization;
* complete state loss producing a new device lineage;
* divergent recovery profiles;
* stale external anchor evidence;
* sender and receiver device retirement;
* relay retention without receipt promotion;
* exact event identity across multiple recipient envelopes.

The sixteen malformed-state cases include mutated retry bytes, altered logical-event identity, mismatched room policy, wrong recipient device, unknown session, counter regression, excessive skip, unauthenticated state mutation, profile-head rollback, divergent-chain merge, receipt carrying secret material, and a removed device appearing in new fanout.

The model’s state is deliberately synthetic and public. It contains labels, counters, digests and expected statuses—not operational private keys. No result should be used as a secret or copied into a production session.

### 131.10 Remaining decisions and recommendation

Vaultglass closes one implementation gate and exposes the next ones more sharply. It does not answer who may publish a device prekey, which service is authoritative for one-time reservation, how a remote fetch is authenticated and freshness-checked, how service replication avoids double reservation, how depletion and abuse are bounded, how device retirement propagates, how session-state settlement and prekey consumption become one recoverable transaction, or how a pairwise ratchet is constructed and migrated.

The recommendation remains the **focused review branch** before adding a network authority. Freeze Keyglass and Vaultglass. Review the domain separators, signed coordinates, first-payload transcript, reservation/settlement ordering, journal envelope, crash points, restore rule, last-resort semantics, and external-witness assumptions. Turn findings into deterministic negative fixtures. Only after that should a loopback-only reservation laboratory be considered.

A future reservation laboratory should still bind only to loopback by default, have a separately administered head witness, use exact compare-and-set semantics, retain permanent tombstones, inject failure before and after each persistent phase, expose depletion/fork/rate metadata honestly, and have no chat integration. Candidate existence must never imply permission to publish. Publication must never imply a successful remote reservation. Reservation must never imply a valid session. A valid session must never imply the first payload was durably accepted. Every one of those edges needs its own evidence.

### 133.1 The composition lane

The altered-ciphertext fixture is intentionally public and synthetic. Its purpose is to make one ordering error difficult to ignore. A signed KEM ciphertext can be authentic as a sender statement while still producing the wrong candidate secret at the receiver. ML-KEM decapsulation returning thirty-two bytes does not authenticate the application transcript. The first AEAD result is the application confirmation in this reviewed target. Until that succeeds, there is no plaintext to expose, no ratchet/session state to commit, and no one-time candidate to consume.

This result does not prove that the proposed v2 is complete, secure, deniable, interoperable, constant-time, live, rollback-resistant, forward-secure, post-compromise secure, or suitable for deployment. It does not establish an authoritative remote reservation service or distributed transaction. It does not independently review the carried implementation. It shows that the named v1 seams exist and that the proposed refusal points can be executed with the exact carried providers.

### 133.2 The metadata finding

The most important prose correction in this revision is small enough to be missed in a code review: **authenticated metadata remains disclosed metadata**. The v1 field `first_payload_sha256` is placed in the signed clear header and used as AEAD associated data. RFC 5116’s distinction applies directly: associated data is authenticated but is not encrypted. The field therefore reveals equality and can support dictionary testing for a predictable first message. Signing it more strongly would not make it secret.

The v2 target removes the plaintext-derived digest. When a public diagnostic identity is genuinely needed, a ciphertext digest can be considered under a separately stated purpose and privacy analysis. Even then, a digest is an identifier, not harmless decoration. The constitution now carries this rule so later officers do not reintroduce the leak while attempting to add observability.

### 133.3 Context, authority and settlement coordinates

Seamglass separates three coordinates that v1 leaves too implicit.

**Application context.** A device-to-device initiation must say why it is authorized. For a room, that means the exact room identity and exact owner-signed policy head under which sender and recipient are members. For a pairwise session, it means a narrowly named purpose. Contact pinning is not room membership. A current room name is not a policy identity. A later policy must not retroactively authorize an earlier initiation.

**Reservation authority.** A random-looking token cannot prove that an authoritative service performed one compare-and-set reservation. The future receipt target names the authority, scope, prekey, prekey kind, reservation identity, serial or head, issue time, expiry and signature. Static mirrors may distribute reusable last-resort material, but they cannot turn it into a one-time reservation by assertion.

**Durable settlement.** A candidate-prekey transition cannot be settled by an opaque digest unrelated to the resulting session. The future intent binds the exact prekey and reservation, session-init identity, transcript digest, first-ciphertext digest, resulting durable session/ratchet head and disposition. Settlement is not complete merely because decryption succeeded in memory. Conversely, a lost acknowledgement after durable settlement is reconciled by exact operation identity rather than by inventing a second consume transition.

These are proposed v2 review coordinates, not deployed wire compatibility. New domains are required. A v1 signature must never be reinterpreted as v2 authority because a parser happens to find familiar fields.

### 133.4 Failure ordering and state custody

The target processing order is now explicit:

1. admit bounded canonical bytes;
2. verify user/device authorization and the sender-device signature;
3. verify the exact recipient and application context;
4. verify publication and the authoritative reservation receipt;
5. decapsulate the candidate KEM secret;
6. derive keys under new context-bound domains;
7. authenticate and decrypt the first payload;
8. prepare the durable session/ratchet state;
9. atomically settle candidate custody together with the exact durable session head;
10. only then expose plaintext or emit an acknowledgement.

Any parse, signature, authorization, context, reservation, KEM-processing, KDF, AEAD or durable-commit error discards candidate session changes. The local candidate remains in the exact state justified by durable evidence. A reserved candidate is not silently returned to available inventory after ambiguity. A consumed candidate is not republished after restore. A reusable last-resort candidate remains visibly reusable and is governed by exact-init deduplication, rate limits and rotation rather than one-time language.

The ordering borrows discipline from the reviewed primary sources; it does not claim protocol compatibility with Signal PQXDH or Sesame. Those sources are precedents for binding identity/context, aborting after failed initial authenticated decryption, delaying one-time deletion until success, and discarding state changes on errors. Vibechat still owes its own complete construction, analysis and implementation evidence.

A directory publication is not a reservation. A reservation is not a valid session. KEM output is not authenticated first-payload success. Successful decryption in memory is not durable settlement. Durable settlement is not acknowledgement delivery. A room-policy adoption is not human reading or consent. A reusable fallback is not one-time. ### 135.2 Exact admission, authority, and context

The new records are not extensible bags of JSON. Contextglass applies the already-carried raw-JSON and canonical-wire disciplines to the proposed session seam:

* input is decoded with duplicate-member rejection, safe-integer limits, finite depth, bounded encoded size, valid Unicode scalar handling, and exact canonical JSON comparison;
* every format has one exact field inventory;
* required fields cannot be omitted or replaced with a value of another JSON type;
* forbidden fields are refused;
* unknown fields are refused rather than ignored;
* signatures are verified under the record’s exact versioned domain;
* a v1 signature is never reinterpreted as v2 authority;
* room context is accepted only with an exact room/epoch/policy authorization path covering both user and device identities;
* pairwise context is a separately bounded purpose, not a room-policy shortcut;
* contact pinning is not room membership or device authorization;
* relay delivery, ciphertext custody, invitation acceptance, policy adoption, session acceptance, durable settlement, acknowledgement, and human reading remain distinct events.

The reservation receipt is signed by the configured reservation authority under `Vibechat/prekey-reservation/v2\0`. The session-init is signed by an authorized sender device under `Vibechat/session-init/v2\0`. The exact public header also becomes first-payload associated data. The acknowledgement is signed by the committed recipient device under `Vibechat/session-settlement-ack/v1\0` and is reconstructed only from committed coordinates.

The v2 session header explicitly refuses `first_payload_sha256`. A digest derived from plaintext does not become confidential merely because it appears inside signed metadata. The exact ciphertext is instead bound into the transcript and settlement coordinates. Associated data is authenticated and disclosed; it is not encrypted. Contextglass keeps that distinction explicit.

The corpus also rejects a one-time receipt that disclaims exclusivity, a room context that does not authorize both identities, a pairwise purpose outside the bounded vocabulary, an omitted first-ciphertext digest, an acknowledgement for another durable state head, and an exact record with any undeclared field. Passing these cases is evidence that the verifier enforces this packet’s declared contract, not evidence that all possible malformed encodings or protocol attacks have been exhausted.

### 135.3 Transaction, crash, replay, and acknowledgement boundaries

The twenty transition cases exercise the proposed pure state machine from publication through reservation, authenticated first payload, prepared durable state, local commit, acknowledgement, replay, failure, and recovery. The corpus distinguishes one-time candidates from reusable last-resort candidates rather than giving both an ambiguous `used` flag.

For a one-time candidate, an accepted reservation is exclusive and settlement permanently consumes the candidate. A committed replay returns the exact acknowledgement without another advance. A different transcript, ciphertext digest, session identity, settlement identity, or durable head is not an idempotent replay. A failed KEM/AEAD path does not acknowledge or consume the candidate. An expired or mismatched receipt is not silently refreshed into authority.

For a last-resort candidate, the long-lived candidate may remain reusable, but each accepted session still has a unique reservation/session/settlement lineage. “Reusable” is not permission to reuse a settlement, transcript, operation identifier, IV, message key, or acknowledgement across sessions.

The local durable operation binds:

```text
exact prekey and reservation
exact reservation receipt
exact session-init identity
exact transcript digest
exact first-ciphertext digest
exact prepared session-state head
exact operation identifier and scope
```

The preferred implementation shape is one transactional store or one write-ahead intent whose recovery makes encrypted prekey custody and encrypted prepared session state advance together. The memorandum intentionally does not mandate SQLite, but it adopts exact commit/recovery vocabulary informed by SQLite’s atomic-commit account. A memory-only update cannot support the same crash-durability claim. A successfully decrypted plaintext held only in memory is not a durable settlement.

The four installation labels remain explicit:

```text
unanchored-authenticated
anchored-current
stale-behind-witness
rollback-or-fork-detected
```

An authenticated local journal can establish internal lineage under its local key; it cannot by itself prove that it is the newest state. A separately administered observed head can identify a stale descendant or incompatible branch only within its own availability, authentication, and administrative boundaries. Restoring a journal and its copied witness together is useful recovery, not an independent rollback anchor.

The acknowledgement is not emitted before local commit. Exact committed replay reconstructs the same acknowledgement without state advance. A lost acknowledgement can therefore be retried without pretending the session did not commit. A different state head or settlement identity is refused. Receipt of the acknowledgement tells the sender that the named recipient device signed the named committed coordinates; it does not prove secure deletion, human reading, current room-policy freshness everywhere, or uncompromised endpoints.

### 135.4 Public synthetic cross-provider vector

The Contextglass fixture intentionally publishes every deterministic secret and intermediate required for reproduction: seeds, expanded private keys, public keys, reservation-authority key, device keys, ML-KEM shared secret, transcript input and digest, HKDF inputs and outputs, IV, first ciphertext, plaintext, policy, authorization, receipt, settlement, prepared state head, and acknowledgement. Those values are permanently unsuitable for operational use.

The native OpenSSL/argon2-cffi implementation and the actual carried TypeScript/WASM worker independently reproduced the fixture. The lane verified:

* reservation-authority ML-DSA-65 signature verification;
* sender-device v2 session signature verification;
* recipient-device committed acknowledgement verification;
* ML-KEM-768 decapsulation agreement;
* transcript-bound first-payload key agreement;
* transcript-bound root-key agreement;
* exact AES-256-GCM first-payload decryption;
* context mutation causing first-payload authentication failure;
* failed authentication leaving the pure transaction at `reserved`;
* refusal to emit acknowledgement before commit;
* exact committed replay returning the same acknowledgement without advance.

The vector is useful because it forces the native and worker providers to agree on bytes at the application seam, not merely on primitive output lengths. It is still not a formal proof, independent implementation review, constant-time analysis, side-channel evaluation, entropy assessment, browser-sandbox proof, secure-erasure demonstration, standards validation, production randomness test, remote exclusivity result, or claim that two providers cannot share the same conceptual bug.

The current chat path remains unchanged. It still encrypts each room event independently to current policy recipients with long-term ML-KEM-768 recipient wraps, signs the event with ML-DSA-65, and protects the payload with AES-256-GCM. Contextglass does not make that current envelope forward-secure, post-compromise-secure, deniable, one-time, remotely reserved, or ratcheted.

### 135.9 Remaining decision and next recommendation

The next bounded branch is **authority and federation review before any reservation service**.

Contextglass says exactly what an acceptable receipt, session-init, settlement intent, and acknowledgement must contain. It does not decide who runs the authority, how authority keys rotate, whether a room owner delegates authority, whether more than one writer is legal, how replicas behave during partition, how serial/head compare-and-set works across federation, how expiry is interpreted under clock skew, how already-issued receipts survive authority compromise, how depletion metadata is protected, or how a client proves that a response is current rather than merely well signed.

The next inert memorandum should specify and test:

1. one exact authority identity and scope for each device-prekey publication lineage;
2. authority signing-key rotation, compromise, retirement, and descendant lineage;
3. serial/head compare-and-set semantics and exact idempotency keys;
4. permanent one-time tombstones and bounded last-resort reuse;
5. duplicate request, timeout, lost response, late response, retry, and cancellation behavior;
6. clock source, issue/expiry representation, maximum skew, and no-clock failure behavior;
7. stale replica, partition, fork, restoration, and reconciliation rules;
8. rate, depletion, enumeration, metadata-privacy, and abuse boundaries;
9. federation as either single writer, explicitly delegated writers, or explicitly unsupported multi-authority operation;
10. separately administered observed-head options and the limits of each trust domain;
11. crash injection before and after every persistent phase;
12. exact negative fixtures distinguishing publication, delivery, reservation, authenticated session acceptance, durable settlement, acknowledgement, and newest-state evidence;
13. no public bind and no automatic chat integration by default;
14. an explicit refusal to call a loopback laboratory a production reservation service.

The recommended first laboratory remains **one explicit authority per device-prekey publication lineage**. Do not attempt multi-authority exclusivity by optimistic merge. Do not connect the laboratory to live room sending until the authority memorandum, negative corpus, crash corpus, and an independent review of the exact v2 cryptographic composition and adapted browser implementation exist.

A directory publication is not a reservation. A signed reservation is not a valid session. KEM output is not authenticated first-payload success. Successful decryption in memory is not durable settlement. Durable settlement is not acknowledgement delivery. A signed acknowledgement is not human reading or global freshness. A locally authenticated old journal is not newest state. Each edge remains a separate claim with separate evidence.

Loopglass is the first revision in this line that runs a real authority-shaped network surface rather than only carrying an inert authority contract. The distinction is narrow and deliberate. The surface is private, literal-loopback, capability-gated, single-writer, bounded, synthetic, and disconnected from every chat path. It exists so an officer can exercise the Headglass reservation rules against durable bytes and process failure without quietly converting a development experiment into a service.

The manifest binds the complete HTML/shell frame and every named source member carried inside it. That gives an exact local byte identity.
