### 139.1 What became executable

The native tool now has an explicit authority-laboratory family:

```text
bash Vibechat.html authoritylab
bash Vibechat.html authoritylab --full
bash Vibechat.html authority-lab-new --directory ABSENT_PRIVATE_DIRECTORY
bash Vibechat.html authority-lab-inspect --directory PRIVATE_DIRECTORY
bash Vibechat.html authority-lab-serve --directory PRIVATE_DIRECTORY --port 0 --ready-file ABSENT_READY_FILE
bash Vibechat.html authority-lab-request --directory PRIVATE_DIRECTORY --url LOOPBACK_URL --prekey PREKEY_ID --operation OPERATION_ID --ttl SECONDS --request-output ABSENT_FILE
bash Vibechat.html authority-lab-cancel --directory PRIVATE_DIRECTORY --url LOOPBACK_URL --request-file REQUEST_FILE --operation OPERATION_ID --ttl SECONDS --cancel-output ABSENT_FILE
bash Vibechat.html authority-lab-call --directory PRIVATE_DIRECTORY --url LOOPBACK_URL --input EXACT_SIGNED_RECORD
```

Creation requires an absent private directory. It writes exactly bounded local custody objects: an encrypted authority journal, a private journal key, a private capability token, synthetic root/writer/requester seeds, a signed-head anchor, a public synthetic bootstrap, and a private writer lock. The directory is explicitly reduced to mode `0700`; private files are mode `0600`. The tool does not treat an inherited setgid bit, group-readable parent, existing path, symlink, or world-readable secret as harmless.

Serving is explicit. The listener binds the IPv4 literal `127.0.0.1`, requests an ephemeral port by default, and does not opt into `SO_REUSEADDR` or `SO_REUSEPORT`. There is exactly one application route:

```text
POST /v1/authority
```

There is no GET route, list route, inventory route, discovery route, browser route, CORS allowance, cookie flow, URL capability, or background daemon. A request must carry the exact private capability in an `Authorization: VibeCap …` header. The capability bytes do not enter the URL, ready receipt, cookie store, browser storage, source tree, public bootstrap, response body, or ordinary log. Literal loopback and a secret header are separate controls: loopback narrows routing; it does not establish caller identity by itself.

The journal uses authenticated whole-file encryption and exact canonical records. One nonblocking advisory lock owns the writer. Mutation follows temporary-file write, file fsync, atomic replacement, and directory fsync. An authenticated signed-head anchor remains separate from the encrypted journal so a restored old but internally valid journal can be recognized as rollback. A descendant may heal the anchor. A signed divergent head is quarantined as a fork rather than merged, selected by timestamp, or relabeled newest.

The implemented authority semantics remain those reviewed in Headglass:

- serial and prior-head compare-and-set are exact;
- operation identifiers are idempotency coordinates, not reusable labels;
- an exact committed replay returns the exact saved response bytes;
- reusing one operation identifier for different intent is refused;
- one-time candidates move through availability, reservation, settlement, cancellation, expiry, and permanent tombstone rules without resurrection;
- cancellation wins only under its exact authenticated race conditions;
- a late cancellation cannot recreate availability after a completed settlement;
- last-resort material is explicitly nonexclusive and bounded rather than called one-time;
- public errors collapse unknown, unavailable, reserved, depleted, expired, cancelled, and retired targets rather than exposing inventory;
- no response claims that a human read anything, that the authority is globally current, or that a remote peer settled a session.

The browser client and carried cryptographic worker contain no authority-laboratory route. Browser chat, terminal chat, room policy, profiles, relays, WebRTC signaling, TURN issuance, courier delivery, receipt discovery, prekey custody, and session setup do not call the laboratory. An officer must opt in at the native command line and must carry its private directory separately from the public three-file release.

### 139.2 Crash and restart evidence

The direct Loopglass lane passed 49 assertions before the carrier was sealed. The finished carrier lane passed 53 because it additionally exercised the carried memorandum surfaces and the native `authority-lab-new` and `authority-lab-inspect` commands.

The crash corpus covers twelve named persistence boundaries. Reservation is interrupted before write, after temporary-file fsync, after replacement, and after directory fsync. Cancellation is interrupted at the corresponding phases. Creation has its absent-or-valid boundary. Uncertain response delivery is replayed after restart. The checks distinguish an old committed state from a new committed state rather than declaring every injected exception equivalent.

The resulting claims are intentionally limited:

- before replacement, restart observes the old committed journal;
- after replacement, restart observes the new committed journal even if the caller did not receive a response;
- repeating the exact operation after uncertain response returns the saved response without appending a second transition;
- a mismatched retry is refused;
- a stale restored journal is refused by the external signed-head anchor;
- an exact descendant can advance and heal the anchor;
- a divergent signed head is quarantined and not merged;
- a second writer cannot acquire the existing live directory;
- no crash test proves disk firmware behavior, filesystem correctness under every mount option, power-loss behavior on every platform, remote durability, or secure erasure.

The tests use ordinary Linux file and locking semantics available in the current environment. They do not convert `os.replace`, fsync, or `flock` into a distributed transaction. They do not claim that a copied private directory is singular, that a host clock is trustworthy, or that loopback traffic is invisible to every local observer.

### 139.3 A cross-revision defect found by full replay

Running the complete predecessor chain found a defect that had been latent behind edition advancement. Vaultglass’s encrypted prekey-custody document is a fixed `rev0017` protocol object, and the embedded TypeScript inspector correctly continued to require that revision. The native implementation had reused the carrier-wide `REV` constant, so creating the same custody format under rev0021 labeled it `rev0021`. Native code could read what it had written, but the actual carried worker refused the mismatched protocol coordinate.

The repair introduces a dedicated `PREKEY_CUSTODY_REVISION = "rev0017"` constant for that on-disk format and its redacted inspection record. Carrier edition and protocol-format revision are now separate coordinates. This is not merely a test accommodation: silently advancing a durable private-state version without a migration rule is exactly the kind of ambiguity the project’s versioned domains are meant to prevent.

Because `native.py` changed, every dependent review object was regenerated in dependency order. The deterministic protocol packet, malformed-input corpus, raw-JSON admission corpus, Wayglass ratchet memorandum, Keyglass device/prekey memorandum, Vaultglass custody memorandum, Seamglass composition review, Contextglass session-settlement memorandum, Headglass authority memorandum, and Loopglass laboratory memorandum all received fresh source bindings. ### 139.6 Research performed this turn

Online research was performed again, as the constitution requires. Six new primary-source records were carried as T113–T118:

5. Python and Linux atomic-replacement semantics were reviewed to bound what `os.replace` can establish locally and what still requires file and directory fsync.
6. SQLite’s atomic-commit, rollback-journal, hot-journal, and WAL documentation was reviewed as a comparison point for crash recovery. Loopglass does not claim SQLite semantics; its much smaller journal states its own exact phases.

### 139.7 What Loopglass does not establish

Loopglass is not a production reservation authority. In particular, it does not establish:

- safety against another local process that can read the private capability or key files;
- safety on a hostile or multi-tenant host;
- public-network authentication, TLS termination, DNS identity, firewall policy, or service discovery;
- reliable exclusive one-time behavior across copied directories, virtual-machine snapshots, multiple hosts, or authorities;
- consensus, quorum, leader election, delegated writers, multi-region failover, or live federation;
- external authenticated time, bounded real-world clock skew, or proof that an expiry decision used correct time;
- transparency-log consistency, witness diversity, or globally newest state;
- metadata anonymity, traffic-analysis resistance, or secrecy from the operating system;
- remote secure deletion, local secure erasure, or recovery resistance after media copying;
- forward secrecy, post-compromise security, deniable authentication, pairwise ratcheting, group ratcheting, MLS compatibility, Signal compatibility, or HPKE compatibility;
- independent review of the adapted browser cryptography;
- formal protocol proof, implementation audit, penetration test, or production hardening;
- permission to connect the laboratory automatically to chat.

The absence of those claims is not shame. It is part of the object’s constitution. The project records what ran and what remains outside the evidence boundary.

### 139.8 Next bounded recommendation

The next implementation should not be automatic room chat integration. The next bounded object should be a **single-process reservation-to-settlement composition laboratory** using two synthetic local device identities and the exact current formats.

That laboratory should:

1. create or open one Loopglass authority directory explicitly;
2. publish a synthetic device/prekey lineage under its exact root/writer coordinates;
3. obtain one exact signed reservation receipt through the capability-gated loopback route;
4. construct the exact Contextglass v2 session-init header bound to that receipt, room, pairwise identities, device authorizations, KEM ciphertext, transcript, and application context;
5. authenticate the first payload before exposing plaintext;
6. commit local settlement before emitting acknowledgement;
7. submit or reconcile the exact authority settlement/cancellation outcome without resurrecting a one-time candidate;
8. inject failure at every edge between reservation response, KEM processing, payload authentication, local commit, acknowledgement emission, and authority observation;
9. demonstrate exact replay after a lost response and refuse operation-ID reuse with different intent;
10. keep all identities, keys, messages, authority state, relay state, and receipts synthetic and private;
11. expose no browser route, no room-send route, no automatic daemon, and no public listener;
12. produce one explicit transcript that distinguishes publication, reservation, authenticated acceptance, local settlement, acknowledgement, authority observation, and human reading.

Only after that composition laboratory and an independent review of the exact adapted cryptographic implementation should an officer consider a separately permissioned experimental chat adapter. Even then, fallback must be refusal rather than silently returning to long-term static wrapping while claiming ratchet or asynchronous-session protection.

## 141. Rev0022 finished-carrier evidence — Settlementglass

Settlementglass is the first revision in this line to execute the complete private synthetic path that earlier memoranda kept separate: device/prekey lineage, authority reservation, session-init, first-payload authentication, durable recipient settlement, acknowledgement, and later authority observation. The point is not that all messaging problems are now solved. The point is that every transition can be named, interrupted, reopened, and distinguished from the next one before any product route depends on it.

The sealed carrier exercised in this turn has this exact identity:

```text
revision: rev0022
edition: Settlementglass
bytes: 3,488,206
SHA-256: cd50b701c4a3ad1ded5d6d350829c4d64934d896596e705c7a4a188a4118bc7d
named source members: 56
```

The source inventory grew by exactly three members:

```text
vibe-session-lab             session_composition_lab.py
vibe-session-lab-memorandum  session_composition_lab_memorandum.json
vibe-session-lab-tests       session_composition_lab_checks.py
```

No source member was fetched at runtime. No cryptographic module URL was added. The browser worker, WASM bytes, readable TypeScript/C sources, notices, and compiler receipts remain embedded. The new laboratory is native/officer machinery, not a browser dependency.

### 141.1 One exact synthetic lineage

A new lab creates two synthetic user identities and one synthetic device per user, plus responder one-time and last-resort KEM material. The user signing keys authorize their devices. The responder device signs exact prekey records and an exact publication. The publication is installed into one separately created Loopglass authority directory rather than discovered through a network directory.

The tests verify all of these relations before the reservation begins:

- the initiator user identity matches its signing and KEM public material;
- the responder user identity matches its signing and KEM public material;
- each device authorization binds its exact user, device, signing key, installation coordinate, creation time and scope;
- each prekey record binds its exact responder user/device, prekey identifier, KEM public key, kind, expiry/use bound, publication coordinate and device signature;
- the publication binds the exact set and ordering of carried prekeys;
- the authority inventory uses the exact one-time record identity;
- the authority publication coordinate equals the exact device publication identity;
- the authority recipient is the exact responder user/device;
- the authority requester key is the initiator device signing key.

The public objects are synthetic fixtures. The private seeds remain outside public summaries and delivery ZIP members. Nothing in the carrier claims that these fixtures are real accounts, remote users, provider inventory, or permission to publish somebody’s operational keys.

### 141.2 Reservation intent is durable before the request leaves

The lab first writes a local operation record naming the exact intent, application context, room/direct-chat context, selected publication, intended recipient, expected authority coordinate, and stable operation identifier. Only after that intent is durable does it send the signed reservation request to the owned Loopglass route.

This order means a crash before network action and a crash after network action can be told apart. It also supplies a local comparison object if a later run presents the same operation identifier with a different intent. Such a changed local intent is refused before a second reservation, KEM operation, or session-init is attempted.

The authority request remains an exact Headglass/Loopglass object. Capability possession admits the HTTP transport; the requester-device signature and authorized requester key admit the application action. Literal loopback remains routing scope, not identity. The response is a signed reservation receipt or a signed bounded refusal, not an unsafely inferred inventory record.

### 141.3 The reservation response is persisted before cryptographic session construction

A returned reservation response is not used only from volatile memory. Settlementglass persists the exact response bytes, response digest, authority scope, serial, head, selected prekey coordinate, and operation relation before KEM encapsulation and session-init construction.

The `after-authority-response-before-local-record` crash point is therefore important: the authority may already have committed a reservation while the local journal lacks the response. On restart, the lab repeats the exact canonical signed request. Loopglass identifies the already-durable operation and returns the exact saved response bytes. No second reservation is appended. This remains true if the restart occurs after the original request’s admission window closes.

That behavior required a specific repair to the Loopglass handler. New admission and exact durable replay now use separate clock decisions. The authority first authenticates and shapes the exact record sufficiently to locate an existing operation and compare its digest. If the exact operation already exists, the saved response is replayed. If it does not exist, the current admission clock and all normal preconditions apply. Different bytes do not inherit the old operation’s replay privilege.

The resulting rule is narrow:

```text
same operation + same canonical signed request bytes + durable prior result
    -> exact saved response replay

same operation + different admissible canonical request bytes
    -> signed idempotency conflict

new operation or no durable result
    -> current admission clock and ordinary authority rules
```

This is not a general license to ignore expiry. It exists to recover an already committed result without performing a second mutation.

### 141.4 Contextglass v2 remains the exact session coordinate

After the exact reservation is locally present, the initiator encapsulates to the selected one-time ML-KEM-768 public key and constructs the exact Contextglass v2 session-init. The object binds, among other fields:

- protocol and record format;
- exact initiator and responder user identities;
- exact initiator and responder device identities and authorizations;
- exact responder prekey record and publication coordinate;
- exact Loopglass reservation identity, authority scope, serial and head;
- exact KEM ciphertext;
- exact application context (`direct-chat/v1` in this lab);
- exact transcript identity and signature domain;
- the initiator-device signature.

At the responder, device authorization, publication membership, reservation identity, recipient coordinates, session signature, KEM decapsulation, transcript derivation and expected context are checked before the first payload can advance. These checks exercise the current carried providers; they do not constitute a side-channel review, proof of key indistinguishability, or validation of the adapted browser implementation.

### 141.5 First-payload authentication is not yet plaintext release

The first payload is encrypted under key material derived from the exact KEM/session transcript and authenticated with AES-256-GCM. A successful open establishes that the exact ciphertext and associated data match the derived key in this run. The lab still does not expose the plaintext to application state immediately.

Instead, it records `payload-authenticated` and prepares the settlement transaction. The plaintext is held only as candidate process memory while the durable commit is pending. The journal receives no plaintext token. Application eligibility is represented by a bounded release count and exact digest-bound state.

The negative fixture signs a valid session/first-payload structure but supplies unauthentic ciphertext. The responder refuses it. The finished-carrier checks establish:

- the invalid AEAD path returns `payload-rejected`;
- plaintext release count remains zero;
- no settlement identity is installed;
- no acknowledgement is created;
- the authority-reserved one-time prekey is not made available again;
- replay of the failed payload does not cross the settlement boundary.

A signed message is not automatically authentic encrypted content. A successful KEM is not automatically successful application data. Those boundaries remain visible in code and receipts.

### 141.6 The local commit is one exact settlement boundary

The settlement commit installs four related facts together inside the encrypted recipient journal:

1. the selected one-time prekey changes from local available custody to a permanent consumed tombstone;
2. the exact active session head becomes current for this local synthetic pair;
3. the exact settlement identity derived from canonical settlement intent is retained;
4. exactly one first-payload release eligibility is recorded.

The settlement identity is:

```text
sha256("Vibechat/prekey-settlement/v2\0" || canonical settlement intent)
```

The commit uses the existing same-filesystem whole-file journal helper: serialize canonical state, encrypt with AES-256-GCM, write a private temporary file, fsync the file, replace the journal, and fsync the directory. The application tests observe states before and after this boundary. They do not claim multi-file atomicity for seed/key files, a transaction across the authority directory, immunity to full-directory rollback, or universal power-loss behavior.

Once this commit exists, exact replay never increments the release count beyond one. A crash after commit but before acknowledgement is therefore distinguishable from a crash before commit. Restart reconstructs missing post-commit records from the committed coordinates rather than reopening cryptographic acceptance or releasing plaintext again.

### 141.7 Acknowledgement is exact device state, not human reading

The responder acknowledgement is created only after local settlement commit. It binds the exact session and settlement identities under the acknowledgement domain and is signed by the exact responder device key. The acknowledgement is then persisted in the same private composition record.

The tests verify the signature using the responder device public key. They also verify ordering: first authenticated acceptance precedes durable settlement; settlement precedes acknowledgement. If a crash occurs after commit and before acknowledgement, restart reconstructs the acknowledgement without creating another settlement or release.

Every protocol event carries `human_reading_observed=false`. Completion, acknowledgement, authority observation, replay, and inspection never change it. The acknowledgement means only that the exact responder device process committed the exact settlement state represented by the signed record. It does not establish that a person saw, read, understood, approved, consented to, or will retain the message.

### 141.8 Authority observation remains a later read

After acknowledgement, Settlementglass inspects the authority’s exact current head and prekey state. The expected observation is that the selected one-time candidate remains unavailable under the durable reservation/tombstone rules. That observation is retained with the composition transcript.

The observation is deliberately not folded into the recipient’s local atomic commit. The recipient can settle locally even if the later observation has not yet been written. A crash after acknowledgement but before observation restarts at the observation step. A crash after observation but before the final complete marker retains the observation and finishes without duplicating earlier work.

The authority observation is exact for the owned local authority directory at that time. It is not evidence that no copy of the directory exists, no other authority was created, no snapshot can be restored, or the observed head is globally newest.

### 141.9 Ten crash edges and exact restart convergence

The direct and finished-carrier Settlementglass lane injects all ten named edges. For each one, the test performs the interrupted run, inspects durable state, restarts with the exact same operation and intent, and checks two central invariants:

- the operation converges to one complete result;
- the authority records one reservation, not a second one.

The edges cover every important handoff in the current single-process sequence:

| Crash ID | Edge | Restart responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| SCL-001 | after reservation intent | send the first authority request once |
| SCL-002 | after authority response, before local response record | exact authority replay recovers saved bytes |
| SCL-003 | after local reservation record | begin KEM/session construction |
| SCL-004 | after KEM, before session record | deterministically rebuild exact session coordinates |
| SCL-005 | after session record, before payload authentication | authenticate the exact first payload |
| SCL-006 | after payload authentication, before prepare | prepare without application release |
| SCL-007 | after prepare, before commit | commit consumed custody/session/release eligibility once |
| SCL-008 | after commit, before acknowledgement | reconstruct acknowledgement from committed state |
| SCL-009 | after acknowledgement, before authority observation | perform later exact authority observation |
| SCL-010 | after observation, before complete marker | mark complete without repeating protocol effects |

The crash injector raises a named development interruption. It does not kill the kernel or simulate every storage failure. The value is state-machine coverage and exact durable reopening, not theatrical claims about hardware power loss.

### 141.10 The coordinate seam blocks product integration

The lab’s most important unresolved result is not a failing test. It is the visible mismatch between two legitimate predecessor identifiers.

Keyglass defines the device identity from user identity and installation nonce. Loopglass authorizes a requester coordinate derived from the requester signing public key. The same synthetic device signing key appears in both records, so cryptographic verification can succeed. But there is no signed carried record saying that this device coordinate delegates this authority-requester coordinate for this scope and time.

Settlementglass refuses to hide that missing relation. The memorandum names it. The public summary exposes both coordinates. The tests require them to remain distinct. The assurance boundary says that passing the laboratory does not authorize product integration until the seam and production authority/storage model receive independent review.

A plausible next object is a signed authorization record with fields such as:

```text
format
user_id
device_id
device_authorization_id
authority_scope
requester_id
requester_sign_public_key
allowed_operation_families
not_before
expires
sequence_or_generation
prior_authorization_id
revocation_coordinate
user_signature
device_signature (if required by the selected model)
```

Those fields are only a design direction, not an adopted wire format in rev0022. The next officer must research and review the relation before freezing bytes.

### 141.14 Decisions adopted and left open

Adopted in rev0022:

1. a first payload must authenticate before settlement preparation;
2. application plaintext release eligibility appears only after durable local settlement;
3. one-time local custody tombstoning, session activation and release eligibility commit together in the composition lab;
4. acknowledgement follows settlement and remains device-state evidence only;
5. authority observation follows acknowledgement as a separate read;
6. exact replay of a durable authority operation may survive admission expiry;
7. changed bytes under the same authority operation do not replay;
8. changed local intent under the same composition operation is refused;
9. every protocol event explicitly refuses human-reading inference;
10. the Keyglass device and Loopglass requester coordinates remain distinct until an authorization rule is reviewed;
11. the laboratory remains private, synthetic, single-process and outside product chat;
12. future turns continue online research and three-file delivery together.

Open after rev0022:

- exact device-to-authority requester authorization and revocation;
- a multi-process composition exercise with independently restarted participants;
- a second filesystem/persistence boundary where available;
- production directory, publication and remote one-time semantics;
- independent review of browser/native PQ and transcript binding;
- an operational pairwise ratchet after the initialization/settlement coordinate is reviewed;
- group-session design and MLS comparison beyond the current pairwise lab;
- secure key rotation and recovery without rollback ambiguity;
- contact-device replacement and authority delegation;
- attachment/session integration under the same durable-admission rule;
- voice/video and live-media PQ application protection;
- public-provider TURN/NAT evidence without overstating trials as permanent free hosting.

The next recommendation remains deliberately smaller than chat integration: freeze an inert authority-requester authorization record and negative corpus first.

The three canonical files travel together. `test.sh` is for development officers; end users do not need an external runner. Its exact bytes also travel inside the HTML so the workshop survives separation. The HTML contains the browser client, Bash polyglot dispatch, native Linux endpoint, blind relay, terminal client, embedded TypeScript/WASM cryptography, readable officer tools, tests, research catalog, constitution, attributed letters, exact selected donor records, deterministic cryptographic review, strict malformed-wire and raw-JSON corpora, the inert Wayglass ratchet memorandum, the inert Keyglass device/prekey memorandum, Vaultglass encrypted local prekey custody, Seamglass’s blocking composition review, Contextglass’s exact proposed v2 reservation/session/settlement/acknowledgement contract, Headglass’s inert single-writer authority contract, Loopglass’s private capability-gated authority crash laboratory, and now Settlementglass’s private synthetic end-to-end composition laboratory. Settlementglass carries one exact Keyglass publication through one exact Loopglass reservation, one exact Contextglass v2 session-init, authenticated first-payload admission, durable local settlement, recipient acknowledgement, later authority observation, crash injection, and exact replay—without wiring any of it into product chat.

### 143.0 Received rev0022 continuation briefing — historical

The owner’s standing phrase authorizes continuation in the current response. It means: recover the current record; read the latest briefing, constitution, exact source identities, evidence, and attributed handoff; **RESEARCH ONLINE EVERY TURN**; choose one coherent bounded improvement; preserve disagreement and stale history; exercise every lane that actually reaches the change; update `Vibechat.html`, `BOOTSTRAPROSE.md`, and `test.sh` together; and return one correctly named three-member ZIP.

It is not a command to work after the response. It does not authorize publication, spending, creation of provider accounts, modification of external infrastructure, transfer of credentials, weakening host safeguards, or automatic revival of every historical proposal. A restored task is evidence to review, not fresh authority to execute.

There is no shame in a missing browser, kernel feature, provider account, compiler, network route, filesystem capability, or test fixture. Pass, fail, and unavailable are different outcomes. An unavailable lane is not a failed assertion, but it is also not a pass. This project records the boundary rather than inventing evidence to make the story cleaner.

### 143.1 The selected rev0022 change — rev0022 historical

**rev0022 is Settlementglass.** Loopglass ended with a precise recommendation rather than a product claim: compose one synthetic publication, reservation, session-init, authenticated first payload, durable settlement, acknowledgement, and authority observation in a private crash laboratory before considering chat integration. Settlementglass implements that recommendation literally.

The carried executable source is `session_composition_lab.py`. Its verifier is `session_composition_lab_checks.py`. Its reviewed machine-readable contract is `session_composition_lab_memorandum.json`. The officer-facing command is `sessionlab`, and `test.sh settlementlab` is a separate lane. These three source identities bring the named carrier inventory to **56**.

The laboratory remains outside the product path. Browser chat, terminal chat, rooms, encrypted profiles, relays, WebRTC, managed TURN, invitation delivery, policy adoption, and ordinary message sealing do not call it. Creating or inspecting a lab starts no listener. A run starts one explicitly owned `127.0.0.1` authority process, uses it inside that command, and stops it before returning. There is no daemon unit, background scheduler, provider account, public hostname, remote directory, or automatic publication.

The current product message path remains the older long-lived ML-KEM-768 recipient-wrap, ML-DSA-65 event-signature, and AES-256-GCM payload design. Settlementglass does **not** silently upgrade product chat to forward secrecy, post-compromise security, deniable authentication, asynchronous production prekeys, or a ratchet. It is a development composition proof-of-behavior for one exact synthetic state machine.

### 143.2 The exact processing order — rev0022 historical

Settlementglass makes the following order explicit and separately observable:

1. validate exact synthetic user, device, prekey, and publication lineage;
2. persist the exact reservation intent locally;
3. send the exact requester-device-signed reservation request to the capability-gated Loopglass authority;
4. persist the exact returned reservation receipt before constructing a session;
5. encapsulate to the exact selected one-time prekey and build/sign the exact Contextglass v2 session-init;
6. verify sender authorization, reservation identity, session signature, KEM transcript, room/application context, and exact responder coordinates;
7. authenticate the first payload with AES-256-GCM while withholding plaintext from application state;
8. persist a settlement-prepared record;
9. atomically commit the one-time consumed tombstone, active session head, settlement identity, and one plaintext-release eligibility;
10. create and persist the responder-device acknowledgement only after that commit;
11. observe the authority head and exact prekey state later, without calling the observation globally newest;
12. mark the exact operation complete, while exact replay returns the same session, settlement, and acknowledgement identities without a second plaintext release.

The sequence is the feature. A successful KEM decapsulation is not yet application admission. A valid device signature is not yet an authenticated payload. A successful AEAD open is not yet durable settlement. A prepared settlement is not a committed settlement. A committed settlement is not yet an acknowledgement. An acknowledgement is not human reading. A later authority observation is not part of the recipient’s atomic commit and is not a global freshness oracle.

### 143.3 Authenticate first; release plaintext only after durable settlement — rev0022 historical

The first payload is deliberately handled in two stages. AEAD authentication produces candidate plaintext inside the process, but the application-visible release count remains zero until the encrypted local journal durably commits all of the following together:

- the exact active session head;
- the exact settlement identity;
- the selected one-time prekey’s consumed tombstone;
- the first-payload digest-bound admission record;
- one and only one plaintext-release eligibility.

A valid sender-device signature paired with an invalid first-payload AEAD tag is refused. That path creates no local settlement, no acknowledgement, and no plaintext release. It also does not resurrect the already authority-reserved one-time prekey. The authority reservation and recipient settlement are separate durable domains; failure after reservation does not mean the candidate becomes available again.

The local journal stores state needed to prove release eligibility and exact identities. It does not retain the synthetic plaintext token itself. The public summary contains no capability or private seed. This is a bounded local confidentiality claim, not secure erasure, operating-system isolation, or protection from the same user account that can read the journal key and seed files.

### 143.4 New admission and exact durable replay are different decisions — rev0022 historical

The Loopglass reservation path now distinguishes two questions that had previously been forced through one admission clock:

**May these bytes begin a genuinely new operation now?** A new reservation request must satisfy the current admission window, exact signature, requester authorization, expected head/serial, field bounds, and one-time availability rules.

**Have these exact canonical signed bytes already produced a durable result?** If an exact operation identifier and exact request digest already name a committed operation, the authority may return the exact saved response bytes even after the request’s original admission window has closed. This is response recovery, not a second admission.

That distinction matters after an uncertain response or delayed client restart. An operation that already consumed authority state must remain recoverable without pretending that its old timestamp authorizes a new mutation. Conversely, replay privilege is not attached merely to an operation label. Reusing the operation identifier with any different admissible canonical body becomes a signed idempotency conflict. A changed local composition intent under the same local operation is refused before a second protocol action.

Settlementglass therefore records three separate outcomes:

- exact new admission under current rules;
- exact durable response replay for already committed bytes;
- conflict or refusal for changed bytes or changed local intent.

Expiry, timeout, restart, lost response, and delayed acknowledgement do not recreate one-time availability.

### 143.5 The Keyglass-device / Loopglass-requester coordinate seam remains open — rev0022 historical

The laboratory composes two predecessor coordinate systems without pretending they are already one.

A Keyglass device identifier is derived from the exact user identity plus an installation nonce. A Loopglass requester identifier is currently derived from the requester ML-DSA public key. In this synthetic composition the same exact device signing key authenticates both roles, but the two identifiers remain visibly distinct in records, validation, tests, and the memorandum.

This is not cosmetic. Silently equating the two hashes would invent an authorization rule that neither predecessor contract defines. Product integration remains blocked on one explicit choice:

- define and sign an authority-requester authorization record that binds the Keyglass device coordinate to the Loopglass requester coordinate; or
- revise the authority contract so its requester coordinate is the reviewed device coordinate directly.

Until that choice receives independent protocol review, the lab’s passing result does not authorize automatic publication, reservation, or session establishment in browser or terminal chat.

### 143.6 Private local custody — rev0022 historical

A Settlementglass laboratory directory contains these private regular files:

```text
session-composition.journal
journal.key
session-composition.anchor.json
session-composition.public.json
session-composition.lock
initiator-user-sign.seed
initiator-user-kem.seed
initiator-device-sign.seed
responder-user-sign.seed
responder-user-kem.seed
responder-device-sign.seed
responder-one-time-kem.seed
responder-last-resort-kem.seed
```

The lab directory and its separate Loopglass authority directory are private. Seed and key files are mode `0600`; private directories are mode `0700`; symlinks and clobbering creation are refused. `session-composition.journal` is an AES-256-GCM whole-file envelope over canonical JSON. Replacement uses the existing same-filesystem temporary-write, file-fsync, atomic-replace, and directory-fsync helper. `session-composition.lock` is a cooperating-process advisory lock, not a distributed lease or hostile same-UID defense.

The separate authority directory retains its own encrypted journal, journal key, capability, root/writer/requester material, signed-head anchor, and lock. There is intentionally no distributed transaction spanning the two directories. Settlementglass records the exact authority response locally, commits recipient state separately, and later observes authority state. The tests show deterministic reconciliation for this one process and one filesystem arrangement; they do not prove atomicity across machines, filesystems, power domains, or copied snapshots.

### 143.7 Ten injected crash edges — rev0022 historical

The carried crash matrix names ten edges rather than treating “crashed somewhere” as useful evidence:

```text
SCL-001  after-reservation-intent
SCL-002  after-authority-response-before-local-record
SCL-003  after-reservation-record
SCL-004  after-kem-before-session-record
SCL-005  after-session-record-before-auth
SCL-006  after-payload-auth-before-prepare
SCL-007  after-prepare-before-commit
SCL-008  after-commit-before-ack
SCL-009  after-ack-before-observation
SCL-010  after-observation-before-complete
```

At each edge, the first command records the named interruption rather than claiming rollback. A later exact run reopens both local domains, reconciles the saved operation, returns one complete result, and demonstrates that the authority recorded only one reservation. If the local settlement was already committed, replay does not increment plaintext release. If acknowledgement had not yet been written, it is reconstructed from committed coordinates. If authority observation had not yet occurred, it is performed as a later read rather than folded backward into the local commit.

These tests do not model simultaneous hostile writers, process memory compromise, every kernel/filesystem fault, storage-controller lies, torn key files, copied full-directory rollback, network partition between real hosts, or Byzantine authority behavior. The narrow result is restart reconciliation across ten named application boundaries under the carried Linux local-file model.

### 143.10 Online research performed this turn — rev0022 historical

The project researched online again, as the constitution requires. Five primary references were added as T119–T123.

**T119 — NIST SP 800-227, Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms.** The final September 2025 publication describes a KEM as establishing shared secret material that is then used with symmetric cryptography for encryption and authentication. Settlementglass therefore records KEM establishment, transcript derivation, AEAD authentication, and durable application admission as distinct events. This is alignment with a conceptual boundary, not NIST validation of Vibechat. Source: `https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/227/final`.

**T120 — Signal PQXDH revision 3.** PQXDH provides a comparison point for asynchronous published prekeys, exact identifiers and signatures, an initial AEAD ciphertext, recipient abort on decrypt failure, and deletion/consumption ordering for one-time material after successful initial processing. Settlementglass uses those ideas as comparison points while keeping a different all-PQ identity/signature scheme, exact Loopglass reservation, and local transaction journal. It claims neither PQXDH compatibility nor PQXDH security properties. Source: `https://signal.org/docs/specifications/pqxdh/`.

**T121 — RFC 9420, Messaging Layer Security.** MLS separates authenticated commit/confirmation processing from later application-data use. Settlementglass borrows only the engineering discipline that authenticated state transition and application plaintext admission should be separately observable. The lab is pairwise, synthetic, and not an MLS implementation or group-security claim. Source: `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9420.html`.

**T122 — SQLite write-ahead logging documentation.** SQLite supplies useful vocabulary for commit records, recovery, checkpoints, and implementation-dependent filesystem behavior. Settlementglass does not import SQLite. The comparison helped make prepared, committed, acknowledged, and observed states explicit in the narrower whole-file encrypted journal. Source: `https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html`.

**T123 — SQLite 3.51.3 release notes, 2026-03-13.** Recent WAL-reset and related correctness fixes reinforce that a storage guarantee depends on exact implementation and version. Importing a database would create a new versioned review obligation, not automatically prove durability. Rev0022 therefore keeps the existing carried local journal for this bounded laboratory. Source: `https://www3.sqlite.org/releaselog/3_51_3.html`.

All **37** investigated WebRTC, signaling, TURN, relay, and hosting options remain in the carried research catalog with their original category and review history. No trial was relabeled permanent free service. No provider account was opened, no credentials were created, and no external infrastructure was modified in this turn.

### 143.11 What Settlementglass does not establish — rev0022 historical

Settlementglass does not establish:

- production chat integration;
- a reviewed device-to-authority requester authorization rule;
- public prekey publication or discovery;
- remote exclusivity of one-time material;
- a multi-process or multi-host transaction;
- consensus, quorum, delegated writers, federation, or failover;
- globally trusted time or globally newest authority state;
- safety if every journal, key, anchor, and observation is rolled back together;
- hostile same-UID isolation, hardware-backed keys, secure deletion, or secure erasure;
- side-channel resistance or constant-time behavior;
- formal protocol proof, implementation audit, penetration test, validation, or certification;
- Signal, PQXDH, X3DH, Double Ratchet, MLS, or HPKE compatibility;
- forward secrecy, post-compromise security, deniable authentication, or group ratcheting;
- human reading, comprehension, consent, approval, or indefinite retention;
- voice, video, screen sharing, or application-layer PQ protection for live media;
- permission to turn the private laboratory into a service.

The absence of those claims is not an apology. It is part of the project’s constitutional accuracy. We can still do excellent work with the exact tools and environment available, and we must not turn missing evidence into either shame or a passing badge.

### 143.12 Adopted decision and next bounded recommendation — rev0022 historical

The adopted decision is to retain Settlementglass as a **private synthetic development gate**, not as a product adapter. Its exact records, source, crash matrix, tests, and memorandum travel with the carrier so another officer can reproduce or challenge the result.

The next bounded revision should define and review the missing **authority-requester authorization record**. It should bind one exact Keyglass device authorization to one exact Loopglass requester coordinate, include scope and validity limits, reject ambiguous key reuse, specify rotation/revocation and rollback behavior, and carry deterministic negative vectors. That object should remain inert first. Only after the coordinate is explicit should a follow-on laboratory repeat Settlementglass with independent processes and, where available, a second filesystem boundary.

Do not wire automatic product chat merely because this single-process laboratory passes. The safe fallback remains refusal, not silent use of the older static-wrap path while claiming asynchronous prekey or ratchet properties.


## 144. Rev0023 Mandateglass — exact requester authorization and the remaining receipt boundary

### 144.1 Arrival, parent identity, and scope selection

The parent archive was extracted without executing recovered shell fragments, and its carried manifest verified 56 named sources. The parent HTML is 3,488,206 bytes with SHA-256 `cd50b701c4a3ad1ded5d6d350829c4d64934d896596e705c7a4a188a4118bc7d`. A baseline authority-lane run passed before the new sources were introduced. The conversation handoff contains repeated promises of an inert device/requester gate, but no delivered successor. Those messages were useful context, not evidence that code already existed.

The new work therefore follows rev0022's own current-first next recommendation: make the relationship between installation identity and authority requester explicit before further composition. This revision neither restarts the project nor silently changes its scope into a general OAuth service. Existing browser/terminal chat and the private authority and settlement laboratories continue to have their received implementation bytes.

Three new source members were sufficient: one executable reference, one public machine-readable review packet, and one verifier/corpus driver. No new root file was added to the release. The workshop is still obtained through the product carrier, and the development runner's external bytes equal its carried source exactly.

### 144.2 The coordinates are distinct, even when the signing key is the same

The relevant identities answer different questions. The pinned user identity names a self-fingerprinted user card. The Keyglass device coordinate names a user-associated installation nonce. The exact device-authorization record names the user's signed permission for that installation and device key. The Loopglass requester coordinate hashes the raw ML-DSA public signing key. The new grant binds those values without claiming they are aliases of one another.

The authority side likewise has separate coordinates: scope, current lineage record, authority-key identity, and compare-and-set head/serial. The recipient side names a user, installation, exact publication, and exact one-time prekey. The application side names either a permitted pairwise purpose or exact room/policy/epoch. Collapsing any pair into a convenient display name loses information the verifier needs.

An important consequence is that the wrapper does not rewrite the inner field named `requester_device`. That older field still contains the signing-key hash. Future code should inspect the exact source contracts rather than infer its meaning from the English suffix “device.” The new record makes the Keyglass installation explicit alongside it.

### 144.3 Exact grant anatomy

The outer grant has exactly `format`, `body`, `signatures`, and `id`. The body has exactly the following fields; unknown members are not extensions in this profile:

```text
v, suite, user, device, device_authorization, requester, requester_key,
authority_scope, authority_lineage, authority_key,
generation, previous, state, reason, not_before, not_after,
actions, target, context, max_request_ms, delegation
```

`target` is exactly `recipient_user`, `recipient_device`, `publication`, `prekey`, and `prekey_kind`. The kind is `one-time`. `actions` equals the single-element array `["reserve-one-time"]`; duplicate actions, cancellation rights, fallback keys, wildcards, and booleans masquerading as integers fail the exact profile.

For an active grant, `signatures` has exactly `user` and `requester`. A revoked successor has exactly `user`. The domains are `Vibechat/requester-authorization/v1/user` followed by NUL, and `Vibechat/requester-authorization/v1/requester` followed by NUL. Both sign the canonical body. The record ID covers canonical format, body, and signatures; it does not hash itself.

An initial active grant has generation one, no predecessor, and reason `bootstrap`. An active successor uses the exact previous ID and next generation with reason `replace`. A terminal successor has state `revoked` and reason `revoke`. Exact replay returns a recorded replay status rather than creating another generation. That replay status is not permission to issue an expired or revoked request.

### 144.4 Exact wrapper anatomy and reference admission order

The wrapper also has exactly `format`, `body`, `signatures`, and `id`. Its body is exactly `v`, `suite`, `authorization`, `request`, and `context`; its sole signer is `requester`. The signature domain is `Vibechat/authorized-reservation-request/v1` followed by NUL. `request` is the complete frozen inner signed record, not an untrusted string pointing elsewhere.

The inner and outer signatures are both checked. Inner requester user/key hash must agree with the grant. Inner authority scope/lineage must agree. Recipient user/device/publication/prekey/kind must agree. Context must agree with both the grant and the independently allowed context. The request window must fit the grant, and the inner expected serial/head must equal the verified local authority snapshot. Valid cryptography does not suppress any of those comparisons.

The raw parser and structure gates run before these decisions. The exact current grant is looked up from reference state, never imported from a request. New admission uses the current local device/authority snapshot and clock checks. Its output carries grant ID, wrapper ID, inner request ID, operation, requester key hash and installation ID with decision `authorized-only-not-reserved`. Nothing in that output has been signed by a remote authority or committed to disk.

### 144.5 What the tests establish about authorization, not just encoding

The memorandum carries 42 named mutation descriptors, RAM-001 through RAM-042. They cover wrong types and number bounds; installation/key-hash mismatches; unknown device authorization; malformed keys; delegated or expanded rights; wrong target/authority/context; invalid state and ancestry; outer/inner requester and target substitutions; stale or forked compare-and-set coordinates; operation identifier shape; and early, empty, excessive, or out-of-grant request windows.

Where a scenario needs a valid signature in order to reach the policy check, the test creates a validly re-signed changed record using the public fixture. A rejection caused only by an invalid original signature would not prove the intended scope rule. Expected refusals assert the reference's exact `Refusal.code`; an arbitrary exception is not counted as a passed malformed-input test.

The wider assertions also cover public packet determinism, user/device/authority signature checks, valid admission, strict raw-wire parsing, room context, user-only revocation, renewal and terminal ancestry, explicit authority succession, fresh-installation replacement, active and historical key aliases, clock uncertainty/backwards time, exact recovery, changed-result integrity, transport authorization, and authenticated-history comparison. These assertions are related and sometimes exercise the same mechanism from multiple directions. They are not independent entropy bits or an aggregate security score.

The finished-carrier checks add real officer command execution, source-binding inspection, full projection, export equality and no-clobber refusal. Static source checks and the unchanged baseline comparison support the “not wired into product” boundary. The new admission state machine itself is Python reference execution, with actual carried-worker ML-DSA signing and native verification. It is not a browser implementation of the authorization ledger.

### 144.6 The alias finding, its fix, and the retained limit

The initial reference retained a mapping from accepted requester-key hashes to user/installation coordinates. That prevents a previously accepted key from being reassigned to another installation after the first grant is known. It was not enough when two active device records already shared a signing key before any grant had been installed.

Finding `MANDATE-001-known-active-key-alias` records that distinction. The current code checks all independently verified locally active device records when admitting an active grant or request. A matching signing key under a different user/installation refuses with `ambiguous-active-device-key`. Accepted history still retains its separate `ambiguous-key-reuse` protection, including revoked predecessors.

Exact user-signed revocation is not blocked by the active-alias check: disabling the exact known grant must remain possible even when the device snapshot is ambiguous. A fresh installation with a fresh key and explicit grant is exercised separately. No result proves that every other process, remote user, or offline archive lacks another copy of the key. The invariant is deliberately about observed authenticated state, not universal key uniqueness.

### 144.7 Revocation can be local without pretending to be globally effective

The user-only terminal record solves one local policy problem: a lost or compromised device should not need to countersign its own exact revocation. It does not solve distribution, remote acknowledgement, reservation races, or authority cutover. The reference can retain a terminal stop after the original lifetime expires, after its device becomes inactive, and after the selected authority changes, because no new reservation is being authorized by that transition.

The remaining authority question is sharper than “did a revocation message arrive?” The next contract must determine which authority lineage/head observed the exact revocation, which new requests are refused after that durable point, which earlier results are recoverable, and what happens after a restored authority journal contradicts a surviving observation. A local wall-clock timestamp alone must not choose the winner of a concurrent durable reservation/revocation race.

This revision does not implement that cutover or attach the local grant ledger to Loopglass. User signatures and an in-memory `revoked-terminal` response cannot stand in for a signed, durably persisted authority observation. The boundary is part of the feature, not a deferred documentation correction.

### 144.8 Recovery and restoration are explicitly modeled, not implemented as custody

`remember_fixture_result` is an intentionally named fixture helper. It first evaluates one new request, then retains its full canonical signed bytes and a small exact result in memory. Calling it twice for one operation refuses before creating a second result. It writes no journal, acquires no process lock, consumes no prekey, and offers no crash guarantee.

`recover` requires independent current transport authorization, an unfenced history, the existing operation, exact complete canonical wrapper equality, and result integrity. It does not create a grant or call new admission again. This lets a preexisting result survive later grant expiry, replacement, and revocation without converting that recovery into renewed permission. A requester who merely possesses a public signed message is not thereby authorized to retrieve another identity's result.

`reconcile_anchor` compares already-authenticated ID prefixes. A missing or older offered prefix cannot erase known state. An extension is not adopted automatically; it still needs validation. A fork fences the reference. This is not a cryptographic verification of an arbitrary restore file, a database migration, or an external rollback witness. An eventual durable adapter needs separate crash, multi-process ownership, rollback, and restart evidence. Settlementglass's existing durable journal evidence cannot be borrowed to fill that gap.

### 144.9 The workshop and historical source-binding discipline

`dev.py` now knows 59 members and understands the rev0023 comparison schema. Comparing the new carrier with rev0022 reports three additions, no removals, the changed workshop/governance records, refreshed bound memoranda, and a changed frame. It does not execute the older carrier. Source/impact commands point the next officer to authorization, prekey, authority, session and carrier checks rather than implying a UI-only change.

The existing ratchet, device/prekey, custody, composition, session, authority, authority-lab, and settlement-lab memorandum bodies were compared against their received equivalents with only `source_bindings` excluded. ### 144.10 Primary research custody

T124 is RFC 9449, sections 4 and 4.3, reviewed at `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html`. Its proof-of-possession/access-control distinction informed separate grant and request checks. Vibechat does not claim to implement DPoP, to issue OAuth tokens, or to inherit that protocol's security analysis.

T125 is RFC 9396, section 2.2, reviewed at `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9396.html`. Its discussion of action/resource details and combinations informed the decision to permit one exact action and one exact target/context rather than an implicit product of rights. This is a deliberate local-profile restriction, not a claim that all possible applications require that scope.

T126 is RFC 9421, sections 7.2.1 and 7.2.2, reviewed at `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html`. Coverage and replay are separate concerns. The new wrapper therefore signs the full inner request and grant/context binding, while recovery separately checks complete saved canonical bytes and transport authorization. It does not implement HTTP Message Signatures.

T127 is RFC 9700, section 2.3, reviewed at `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html`. Audience, resource and action restriction motivated checking the exact current authority and allowed target/action on each new admission. It does not turn the custom reference format into an OAuth access token or confer interoperability.

The date of these reviews is 2026-10-05. The catalog retains 122 technical records with their actual IDs, not an assumption of contiguous numbering. All 37 infrastructure candidates preserve their previous full records. Their price/allowance histories were not marked freshly verified merely because the research file's revision changed.

The wrapper binds the exact grant ID and context to the unchanged inner Loopglass request. The reference checks exact current locally pinned authority scope, lineage and key; exact locally allowed target publication and one-time prekey; exact context; action; current device state; CAS head; bounded half-open times; and both request signatures. A signed scope mismatch is refused, not accepted merely because the cryptography worked. A known active alias for the same public signing key fences new admissions. Historical key-owner records also prevent a revoked key from becoming another installation. Expired grants, inactive devices or changed authority pins cannot make local exact revocation depend on cooperation from a lost device. This is reference behavior, not a claim that every remote authority saw the revocation. Exact result recovery retains the complete canonical wrapper and its signatures, is separately transport-authorized, and creates no new grant or reservation. Older authenticated prefixes retain known revocations; divergent authenticated histories fence new work. Every state in this new module is memory-only conformance state.

### 144.12 The next gate must carry the binding past the admission decision

The exact inner Loopglass request can currently be named by its reservation receipt, but that receipt does not name this new grant/wrapper. Contextglass likewise has a reviewed frozen session/settlement format rather than a slot that can casually absorb new fields. An authorized local reference decision is therefore not an end-to-end authorized session proof.

The next officer should define a new inert admission-binding record, or an explicitly versioned successor after review, whose signatures cover grant ID, wrapper ID, inner request ID, exact authority lineage/head, operation and target, and the relevant authority-observed revocation cutover. Specify recipient verification and refusal of stripped wrappers, mixed grants, crossed authorities, stale observations, contradictory receipts, and altered replay requests. Separate a later read observation from the atomic commit that actually decided admission.

Only after that exact record and refusal corpus are reviewed should an independent-process private lab connect the pieces. Such a lab will need durable authorization and operation custody, crash boundaries, current transport authorization, revival/fencing behavior, and no secret-bearing summaries. Product chat and public services remain out of scope until their own integration evidence exists. Keep the same three-file return discipline and research online each turn.

## 146. Rev0024 Receiptglass — exact authority admission, operation order, and revocation cutover

### 146.1 Received parent, exact selection, and non-selection

The received parent archive is `Vibechat-rev0023-2026.10.05.17.42-mandateglass-exact-requester-authorization.zip`,  with SHA-256 `f3570523c5c5518b19278fdbcbc8f4550201b6882321e2650aa9271449ee1ed2`. It contains exactly the expected three root members. Its HTML is 3,682,627 bytes with SHA-256 `7d22a7be403021299f76be3d4007a33218e58db5a97d05bb9ab80cc33fcd0e5a`, verifies as rev0023, and carries 59 named source members. The parent bootstrap and test driver identities are recorded in section 145.

The parent handoff selected one bounded continuation: carry the new requester authorization through an exact authority admission record and revocation cutover before building an independent-process adapter. That recommendation was accepted. Product chat integration, a public authority, multi-host federation, a new UI, and a general-purpose access-token framework were not selected. The existing browser and terminal product bytes remain the product; Receiptglass is a carried instrument beside them.

The design preserves four predecessor boundaries rather than rewriting them:

1. Mandateglass grant and authorized-wrapper formats remain byte-for-byte predecessor records.
2. Loopglass `vibechat-prekey-reservation-request-v1` retains its original record identity and requester-key coordinate.
3. Headglass `vibechat-prekey-reservation-v2` and `vibechat-prekey-authority-head-v1` retain their existing signature and identity rules.
4. Contextglass session and settlement records retain their existing meanings; Receiptglass does not silently make them authorization receipts.

The new records refer to predecessor IDs and complete frozen records where required. They do not add fields to old bodies and then continue calling the result v1. This matters for deterministic replay, source comparison, recipient verification, and future migration review.

### 146.2 Coordinates carried into one authority statement

The admission record deliberately repeats every coordinate that could otherwise be confused or substituted:

* authority scope, lineage identity, and exact signing-key identity;
* authorization ID, wrapper ID, and unchanged inner request ID;
* requester user identity, Keyglass installation ID, and Loopglass requester public-key hash;
* recipient user identity and installation;
* device-prekey publication ID, exact prekey ID, and `one-time` kind;
* exact pairwise or room context already constrained by the grant;
* request operation ID;
* expected authority serial and signed head before the reservation;
* exact frozen reservation receipt and reservation ID;
* committed authority serial and signed head after the reservation;
* issued, admitted, and expiry times; and
* the explicit admission decision.

The complete field set for `vibechat-authority-admission-receipt-v1` is:

```text
v, suite,
authority_scope, authority_lineage, authority,
authorization, envelope, request, operation,
requester_user, requester_installation, requester,
recipient_user, recipient_device, publication, prekey, prekey_kind,
context,
issued, admitted_at, expires,
expected_serial, expected_head,
reservation_receipt, reservation,
committed_serial, committed_head,
decision
```

The outer record has exactly `format`, `body`, `signature`, and `id`. The signature domain is `Vibechat/authority-admission-receipt/v1` followed by NUL. The record ID covers canonical format, body, and signature with the ID itself omitted. Unknown fields are refused in this profile; they are not treated as harmless extensions.

The verifier does not infer coordinates from convenient labels. It independently validates the grant, wrapper, inner request, reservation receipt, and pre/post heads under their own frozen rules, then cross-checks every repeated value. A changed grant with a fresh authority signature is still refused if it no longer matches the wrapper. A changed wrapper is refused if the inner request identity differs. A changed target, context, expected head, committed head, requester coordinate, or reservation receipt is likewise a different statement and cannot ride on a cryptographically valid but semantically mismatched record.

This is why the bare reservation receipt is insufficient. It can be valid under the predecessor authority contract while saying nothing about the new grant and wrapper. Receiptglass does not retroactively redefine that signature’s coverage.

### 146.3 The operation record is the authority consequence identity

`vibechat-authority-operation-record-v1` gives admission and cutover one shared signed local order. Its exact body is:

```text
v, suite,
authority_scope, authority_lineage, authority,
sequence, previous,
event_kind, event,
authorization, request_operation,
subject_user, subject_device,
prekey_serial, prekey_head,
committed_at
```

`event_kind` is exactly `admission` or `revocation-cutover`. `event` is the exact corresponding record ID. Sequence begins at one, increments without gaps, and names the exact prior operation ID after the first entry. The prekey serial/head is the authority snapshot after the event. The signature domain is `Vibechat/authority-operation-record/v1` followed by NUL.

The separate operation record keeps three questions visible:

* Was the grant and request admitted into one exact reservation result?
* In what order did the authority commit that result relative to revocation cutovers?
* What signed prekey head did the authority claim after the event?

A future durable adapter must settle the event and its operation record together. Receiptglass itself cannot prove that disk atomicity because its state machine is intentionally memory-only. The executable reference therefore treats a missing, mismatched, gapped, or forked operation record as unusable rather than pretending that the signed admission alone is durable enough.

The operation chain is a local total order, not a transparency log. It has no Merkle tree, gossip, cross-operator witness, quorum, or global consistency proof. Its purpose is to make the required authority consequence and ancestry exact before a crash laboratory implements them.

### 146.4 User revocation and authority cutover are deliberately separate records

Mandateglass already defines a terminal user-signed grant successor. That preserves a crucial property: a lost device cannot veto its own revocation. Receiptglass does not add the requester signature back to that terminal statement. Instead, it adds an authority observation.

The exact body of `vibechat-authority-revocation-cutover-v1` is:

```text
v, suite,
authority_scope, authority_lineage, authority,
revoked_authorization, revocation,
slot_user, slot_device,
observed_at,
last_admitted_sequence, last_admitted_operation,
prekey_serial, prekey_head,
state
```

`state` is the cutover state for new work. The authority signature domain is `Vibechat/authority-revocation-cutover/v1` followed by NUL. The record binds the exact user-signed revocation and the exact authorization it terminates. It also binds the last admission prefix the authority says preceded the cutover and the current prekey snapshot. The matching operation record then commits the cutover into the consecutive authority sequence.

The distinction prevents several false claims:

* The user signature does not prove remote propagation.
* The authority cutover does not claim the user signed at the observation time.
* A cutover does not erase an admission ordered before it.
* A valid old authority signature does not prove that its record is newest.
* Exact recovery of pre-cutover committed bytes does not reopen authorization.

The public deterministic fixture exercises both race orders. In admission-first order, the reservation result is retained, a later cutover blocks new work, and exact recovery returns the same committed bytes. In cutover-first order, the proposed admission is refused and cannot manufacture a reservation. Changed-byte retry under the same operation ID is a conflict in either order.

### 146.5 Recipient-side use requires a named local history head

The recipient verifier takes an explicit authenticated operation history rather than silently consulting an unspecified global service. It checks:

1. exact authority pins, signatures, schemas, and record identities;
2. exact grant, wrapper, inner request, target, context, and reservation binding;
3. exact admission-to-operation cross-reference;
4. consecutive operation sequence and predecessor ancestry;
5. the recipient’s exact intended publication, prekey, reservation, sender, and context;
6. the admission’s half-open lifetime; and
7. absence of a later known cutover for the exact authorization/slot in the supplied history.

The verifier refuses a missing history, empty history when the admission claims a sequence, a gap, fork, wrong predecessor, wrong event ID, changed authority coordinate, cutover that predates its supposed admission prefix, or recipient-use fields that differ from the signed binding. It does not fetch a fresher head or infer that none exists.

Finding `RECEIPT-001-local-history-is-not-global-freshness` records the remaining limit. A recipient with an older but internally authenticated prefix may not know that another observer has a later cutover. The correct claim is “valid relative to this retained authenticated prefix,” not “globally current.” A future witness/gossip design may reduce that uncertainty, but importing Certificate Transparency vocabulary without its machinery would make the evidence worse, not better.

### 146.6 Exact recovery remains a distinct action

The reference ledger stores the complete canonical authorized envelope and exact committed result for an admitted operation. Its recovery API requires an exact matching envelope and a separate `transport_authorized` decision. Recovery can succeed after grant expiry or authority cutover only because it returns previously committed bytes; it does not perform policy admission or reserve another prekey.

Changed wrapper bytes, changed inner request bytes, changed signatures, changed operation ID, missing result, or a fenced/divergent history refuse. The one-time reservation remains consumed or tombstoned according to its predecessor record. Recovery cannot make it available again. This preserves Mandateglass C67 and makes the downstream authority consequence explicit.

The reference keeps recovery in memory. It does not claim secure erasure, crash durability, storage encryption, rollback protection, or a private capability endpoint. Those are requirements for the next independent-process laboratory, not accomplishments smuggled into this one through a method name.

### 146.7 Public fixture, malformed corpus, and assertion scope

The memorandum carries a deterministic synthetic public fixture containing:

* one active Mandateglass authorization and its user-signed terminal revocation;
* one authorized wrapper with the complete frozen Loopglass inner request;
* signed Headglass pre- and post-reservation heads;
* the frozen reservation receipt;
* one authority admission receipt and matching admission operation;
* one authority cutover and matching cutover operation; and
* one exact recipient-use statement.

The fixture explicitly warns against real identity, grant, authority, or prekey use. Its keys and records are public test material.

Thirty-three named mutation descriptors cover wrong booleans/integers, suite substitution, authority mismatch, grant/wrapper/request substitution, operation mismatch, requester installation and key-hash substitution, context and target changes, stale compare-and-set coordinates, reservation/head changes, lifetime errors, operation gaps/forks, cutover ancestry errors, and recipient local-history failures. Tests re-sign changed records when necessary to reach the intended semantic refusal. A bad signature alone is not counted as proof of a scope comparison.

The direct pre-seal checker passed 144 assertions. Against the finished carrier it passed 152: the additional assertions exercise the `bindings` summary, complete projection, source-binding equality, all three impact-map entries, byte-exact export, and no-clobber refusal. The predecessor authorization checker passed 148 against the same carrier. These counts include related checks and do not represent independent security bits.

Actual carried-worker ML-DSA signing and native verification are used for the deterministic public records. The ledger and policy transitions are Python reference execution. There is no browser implementation of the Receiptglass ledger, no server adapter, and no claim that passing vectors establish production interoperability.
