### 154.6 Five primary-source reviews this turn

The following are the exact new technical-source catalog records. Earlier research and all infrastructure histories remain above and in `research.json`; these records do not renew old pricing claims.

**T144 — RFC 6960 — status time, next update and response production time**  
Reviewed 2026-10-05. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6960.html  
Status observation, expected next update and signature production are distinct. Sightglass names its committed-history read snapshot rather than treating signature creation as proof of future absence of revocation. This is a design analogy, not an OCSP implementation or a lease.

**T145 — RFC 9654 — current OCSP Nonce Extension, replacing RFC 8954**  
Reviewed 2026-10-05. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9654.html  
RFC 9654 obsoletes 8954, requires extension requesters to use a cryptographically generated nonce of at least 32 octets, and permits up to 128 octets. Sightglass selects a fixed 32-byte random challenge and refuses missing or mismatched query binding. Its own signed-record protocol is not OCSP wire compatibility or compliance.

**T146 — RFC 9421 — HTTP Message Signatures, covered components and replay considerations**  
Reviewed 2026-10-05. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html  
Signature verification alone does not choose application authorization or replay policy. Sightglass separately binds the complete query, purpose, recipient, authority, selected admission, session, settlement and retained prefix, then enforces a live deadline. It reuses no HTTP Message Signatures syntax and makes no conformance claim.

**T147 — SQLite — Isolation In SQLite, snapshot reads and BEGIN IMMEDIATE**  
Reviewed 2026-10-05. Source: https://sqlite.org/isolation.html  
WAL readers retain their transaction snapshot; a later view requires a new transaction. BEGIN IMMEDIATE acquires the writer transaction before subsequent reads. Sightglass defines one bounded read under the existing exclusive Orderglass lock, rolls it back without writes and does not extend that transaction across the participant database.

**T148 — Python time — CLOCK_BOOTTIME and clock_gettime_ns**  
Reviewed 2026-10-05. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html  
The documented Linux CLOCK_BOOTTIME includes suspend time, unlike CLOCK_MONOTONIC. Sightglass uses integer nanosecond elapsed checks alongside the signed wall-time interval and refuses an unavailable elapsed clock. Persisted evidence does not restore a live deadline. Real elapsed-wait checks and synthetic clock controls are not physical suspend qualification.

### 154.7 Constitutional additions C77–C79

**C77 — A fresh authority snapshot is not a recipient-commit lease**

An authenticated latest-observation exchange SHALL name the exact authority read ordering point, the bound request and the locally retained prefix. A fresh challenge and a signed head do not make recipient commit atomic with revocation. Tests and documentation SHALL preserve the race where an unseen cutover occurs after the snapshot but before local commit. A stricter authority-ordered commit policy requires its own explicit protocol and cannot be inferred from an observation timestamp.

**C78 — Retained freshness evidence does not restore live permission**

A prepared or restarted operation SHALL acquire a new challenge for each prospective bounded observation attempt. The local elapsed-time budget SHALL remain an in-process condition and SHALL NOT be reconstructed as reusable permission from retained evidence. Offline, stale, wrong-challenge, incomplete or locally superseded evidence blocks new commitment. Exact recovery of a previously committed result remains separate from fresh work and does not need to renew authorization or rewrite the retained acknowledgement.

**C79 — A refused staged transaction is not a recoverable commitment**

When code stages committed state in memory before the durable transaction, a storage or final-gate refusal SHALL invalidate that handle or fully restore an authenticated prior state. A second call on failed staged memory SHALL NOT manufacture a committed acknowledgement. Transaction tests SHALL check inserted-row rollback and reopen from actual durable state. A time check before COMMIT is not a guarantee that physical persistence or the response completed before the deadline; a stored timing sample must name its actual checkpoint.

## 156. rev0028 Intentglass — selected contract, implementation, findings and handoff

### 156.1 Scope and the rejected alternative

Sightglass established a bounded signed observation at a named authority read point. It did not establish atomicity across the authority and recipient stores. This revision does not add another timestamp and rename it “current permission.” Instead it separates an authority decision from local completion and selects their precedence explicitly. The result is a contract and executable memory-only reference. The parent observer and participant code remain frozen.

The choice trades immediate requester revocation at the recipient's later persistence point for a durable-decision model to be implemented in a later adapter: an authority commit decision which won its order is allowed to finish only its exact prepared work. A later cutover stops undecided work, not that prior decision. This policy must be understood before any product presents it as revocation. It is not a general claim that revocation is ineffective, and not authority for new messages, sessions, prekeys, rooms or installations.

The proposed durable implementation must record the legacy transition and the new event together. Signing both records is insufficient when a crash can persist only one. A separate mirror can describe an incomplete past even when its individual signatures verify. This reference therefore requires creation-only activation and an explicitly pinned complete origin, and refuses to treat an old valid head as automatic activation. It does not implement the authority transaction itself. That omission is the deliberately selected next integration boundary, not an unreported failed attempt to build a service.

### 156.2 Record families and frozen binding rules

| Family | Signer | Exact meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `vibechat-intentglass-origin-v1` | Selected authority | One explicitly pinned creation-only selection after the selected committed admission and preparation. |
| `vibechat-intentglass-commit-intent-v1` | Pinned recipient installation key | Consent to the exact selected preparation, under the selected policy and expected authority prefix. |
| `vibechat-intentglass-abort-v1` | Same pinned recipient installation key | Request to abandon this exact intent before an authority commit decision wins. |
| `vibechat-intentglass-order-event-v1` | Selected authority | One consecutive commit, abort or matching requester-cutover event and its exact request identity/outcome. |
| `vibechat-intentglass-recovery-v1` | Pinned recipient installation key | Bounded read authorization for the exact saved terminal decision, not authority for new work. |

Each new record identity hashes canonical `{format,body,signature}`. Each family has a distinct signature domain. The predecessor formats retain their original identity and signature rules; the new wrapper does not silently rewrite them. Field sets are exact, unknown keys refuse, integer tokens must be safe and must not be booleans, Base64 and lower-case hex remain canonical, and the raw adapter rejects decoded duplicate keys, fractional/exponent tokens, negative zero, invalid UTF-8, surrogate strings and trailing JSON. The raw bound is 262,144 bytes before dispatch. The new-request bound is 30,000 milliseconds; the deterministic selected session uses a narrower interval. Those are reference contract bounds, not a deployed latency service-level promise.

The complete admission must verify under the exact requester and authority trust. Its initial operation is sequence one with no predecessor. Recipient device authorization is verified against the pinned recipient user card. The selected session must carry the real requester installation coordinate rather than substitute the requester signing-key hash. Its sender signature is verified, its header and target match the reservation/admission, and its preparation binds the exact transcript, ciphertext digest and state head. The real recipient's private root and successful authentication remain local prerequisites, not values inferred from authority signatures.

The public fixture uses deterministic synthetic material. Its actual carried worker encapsulates the selected ML-KEM key and produces the first authenticated ciphertext; native decapsulation, derivation and AES-GCM verification agree. A changed ciphertext tag fails native authentication. This cryptographic fixture is separate from the memory-only authorization logic. It does not make public fixture material suitable for an operational identity, and it is not independent audit coverage.

### 156.3 State transitions and equal-time race corpus

The reference ledger begins at the pinned origin with no terminal decision and no cutover. Commit and abort each require the exact expected sequence/head, verified recipient signatures, the selected coordinates and an admitted new-request interval. The authority event must exactly equal the proposed transition and verify under the pinned authority key. All validation and retained-value allocation finish before mutation of the reference order. An accepted event contributes one history entry. Exact replays return saved bytes and do not contribute another entry.

A first commit yields `commit-decided-exact-settlement`. A first abort yields `aborted-before-commit`. A first cutover yields `cutover-blocks-undecided-intents` without falsely reporting successful local cancellation. A cutover may follow either terminal decision, but at most one terminal decision and one cutover exist. Cutover ancestry also verifies the frozen last-admitted prefix and prekey head; an authority-signed false ancestry does not pass merely because it is signed.

All six permutations of commit, abort and cutover are exercised at the same timestamp. Commit/abort/cutover and commit/cutover/abort preserve commit and reject the too-late abort. Abort/commit/cutover and abort/cutover/commit preserve abort and reject commit. Cutover/commit/abort and cutover/abort/commit leave cutover alone and reject undecided work. Each resulting history is independently folded again and checked. Consequently these tests cannot pass merely because conveniently increasing timestamps happen to encode the desired winner.

New work refuses a backwards reference clock, early or expired request, a gap, stale expected head, altered operation identity, changed same-operation bytes or already-decided selection. The exact terminal-recovery path deliberately does not re-admit old work. A separately authorized recovery proof is bounded by the recipient authorization and binds the exact origin and intent. Successful read replay is read-only. An expired or future read proof, wrong signer, wrong intent or absent terminal result does not create a decision.

### 156.4 Recipient interpretation and known-history boundaries

The recipient gate validates the full offered history before accepting it as new knowledge. A shorter prefix refuses without discarding known descendants. A signed conflicting branch fences the gate; the retained earlier branch remains evidence and neither branch becomes automatically authoritative through replay. A duplicate supplied row also refuses: a history position cannot be consumed by an idempotent replay which appended no event. Fork detection is local and requires the conflicting evidence to be observed.

Only an exact matching committed intent can project permission, and only with explicit successful payload authentication, retained exact preparation and no local abandonment. Numeric one is not accepted as a boolean success collaborator. An empty history, signed intent alone, abort event, cutover alone, missing preparation or changed intent is insufficient. An already-decided exact preparation may project permission even when the retained complete history also contains a later requester cutover. That result is the selected policy, not a claim that the requester remains currently authorized.

The recipient gate contains no database writer or acknowledgement generator. It cannot prove exactly-once local application admission, independent role isolation, secure erasure or physical persistence. A later adapter must durably retain preparation before the intent can cross its process boundary, and must durably bind local completion to the decision it consumed. Local abandonment and uncertain sends need retained, auditable states rather than opportunistic fallback to another key. No such adapter is activated by this revision.

### 156.5 Rejected generation, review repairs and dependency closure

The first new fixture-generation attempt stopped before running any conformance assertions: its inherited in-memory active-device set was not JSON serializable. The fixture now carries a sorted list of the identical public identifiers. No trusted membership was added or removed, and no predecessor verifier was loosened. The initial complete corpus then passed 232 direct checks. Adding all equal-time order permutations, independent history refolding and an explicit post-grant-expiry premise expanded the direct corpus to 251 passing checks.

A new-reference code review identified the distinction between idempotent event replay and a supplied history position. The history verifier now compares its resulting sequence against each input row's one-based position. A duplicate-history refusal exercises that guard. This was a correction in the newly written reference before the complete release corpus, not a claim of an inherited production vulnerability.

Updating workshop and driver bytes required refreshing inherited memorandum source bindings. The refresh followed the exact dependency chain through malformed and raw-JSON admission, ratchet, prekeys, custody, composition, session, federation, requester authorization, admission binding and the existing laboratories, ending at Intentglass. All inherited public fixtures remained structurally identical. Only `source_bindings` changed in those older memorandum objects, with the corresponding digest field also changing in the two corpus formats whose digest includes bindings. No test was removed, signature regenerated into a different public fixture, implementation relaxed or old edition relabeled. Settlementglass has no regeneration command; only its exact dependency rows were refreshed while its body remained unchanged.

The final expanded direct corpus was rerun after that refresh. Its 251 source-scope checks are the embedded preseal receipt. The received rev0027 binding lane separately passed 152 checks before integration. Neither is labeled a completed rev0028 carrier run in the embedded evidence. Final carrier and archive evidence lives in section 157 to avoid a recursive self-digest. All prior evidence objects are deep-copied before changing current metadata.

### 156.6 This turn's online primary-source review

The following records are new dated reviews, not revised dates pasted onto older provider claims. The distinction between a source's statement and this project's design choice is explicit. No standards-conformance claim is inferred.

**T149 — RFC 9334 — RATS Architecture, section 10.4 freshness discussion** · reviewed 2026-10-06. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9334.html#section-10.4

The freshness discussion explicitly recognizes that relevant state or appraisal policy can change immediately after evidence generation. Intentglass therefore chooses an authority decision policy instead of claiming that a fresher observation removes the later race. This is design guidance, not remote-attestation implementation or RFC conformance.

**T150 — RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics, section 9.2.2 idempotent methods** · reviewed 2026-10-06. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2

Idempotence describes the same intended server effect for repeated identical requests; retry after uncertain communication requires known semantics. Intentglass separately requires byte-identical saved terminal results and refuses changed bytes under the same operation. No HTTP endpoint, generic POST retry permission or new transport is implemented by this reference.

**T151 — RFC 7009 — OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation, section 2.1** · reviewed 2026-10-06. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009.html#section-2.1

The revocation discussion distinguishes invalidation from possible propagation delay among servers. Intentglass names the authority order at which its requester cutover blocks undecided work. The chosen commit-first completion rule is this project's explicit policy, not a rule borrowed from OAuth or evidence of instant knowledge at another process.

**T152 — SQLite — Atomic Commit, single-transaction recovery and locking assumptions** · reviewed 2026-10-06. Source: https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html

SQLite describes how transaction changes appear all-or-nothing and identifies locking and storage assumptions. A future Intentglass adapter must place frozen cutover and new order event in the same authority transaction, not separate successful commits. This requirement does not create atomicity with a recipient database. No SQLite persistence or crash qualification is added in this inert turn.

### 156.7 Constitutional additions

All 79 received articles remain an exact prefix in the carried constitution. These three additions bring the total to 82.

**C80 — A commit decision is an explicit policy, not a fresher observation**

An authority-ordered recipient commit-intent contract SHALL state which event wins before it is given a listener or a product route. Intentglass selects authority-decision-first/exact-settlement/v1: a commit decision ordered before requester cutover permits only its exact authenticated, retained preparation to complete later; abort-first or cutover-first blocks undecided work. A later cutover does not retroactively undo the earlier decision. This is deliberately not immediate revocation at physical recipient persistence. A signed intent, authority decision, local preparation, local application commit and acknowledgement SHALL remain different claims.

**C81 — Abort and exact recovery do not recycle consumed authority work**

After a send may have occurred, silence SHALL NOT be represented as successful abort, nonexecution, new permission or an unused prekey. An exact terminal decision remains immutable. Separately authorized exact-result recovery SHALL return the retained original bytes without appending new work, refreshing the decision time or switching operation identity. Abort-first blocks the selected intent without releasing or reassigning its reserved one-time prekey; abort-after-commit is explicitly too late. Local abandonment is a local choice, not retroactive cancellation of an authority decision or evidence of secure deletion.

**C82 — One pinned origin, one durable authority order, an explicit local precondition**

The bounded Intentglass reference is creation-only, memory-only and limited to one explicitly pinned complete selection; an arbitrary older signed head SHALL NOT silently activate it. A future adapter SHALL co-commit its new order event and corresponding frozen cutover under the same authority writer lock and transaction, rather than asynchronously mirroring a second journal. A recipient SHALL authenticate and durably retain exact preparation before releasing its intent; an authority signature does not prove this local condition. Complete histories must extend retained knowledge, authenticated forks fence prospective permission, and joint rollback of all observations remains outside local detection. Many-selection activation, recipient key rotation/revocation, endpoint isolation and product integration require separately reviewed gates.

### 156.8 Attributed handoff letter

**letter-0032-officer · Vibechat rev0028 Intentglass continuation officer (assistant) · 2026-10-06**

To the next sandperson: the owner again asked us to run the carried bootstrap and continue. The received rev0027 trio is the parent, not an invitation to infer missing live state. Sightglass's known remaining race is useful evidence: a valid fresh snapshot can precede an unseen cutover and a later successful local commit. I chose to define the meaning of authority commitment before adding another process. Intentglass is an inert exact contract and memory-only refusal corpus, not a fourth listener and not product chat.

The selected policy is authority-decision-first/exact-settlement/v1. A recipient signs its exact intended prepared settlement; the authority orders commit, abort and observed requester cutover. Commit-first authorizes only that already-bound settlement to finish later, including after requester cutover or the original request interval. Abort-first or cutover-first blocks undecided work. There is no promise that revocation can erase a decision which has already won this order, and no claim that the recipient has actually written an application entry merely because an authority signed. This distinction is the point of the revision, not an inconvenience to omit from user-facing language.

Five domain-separated families cover one pinned creation-only origin, the recipient commit intent, a separately signed abort, the authority decision/order event and a separately signed exact-result recovery proof. Twenty-four coordinates retain the seven-member complete Orderglass result, the unchanged frozen signed SessionInit and exact prepared Contextglass settlement, recipient user/installation/key, requester grant/wrapper/key/install, authority scope/lineage/key, reservation, selected prekey/publication and context. Installation and signing-key identity remain distinct. This origin must be an explicit local trust input for a complete creation-only state, not an arbitrary old signed prefix accepted because it looks well formed.

The reference has at most one terminal decision and one matching cutover. All six commit/abort/cutover permutations use the same timestamp and are checked against sequence-based outcomes. Exact terminal replay returns canonical retained bytes and appends nothing. A new nonce cannot reset a decided selection. An abort does not recycle the prekey that Loopglass already reserved. Uncertain sends remain unresolved until exact recovery; an offline authority or missing response is not successful cancellation. Recovery has a distinct recipient signature and bounded read authorization and cannot create work or turn old results into fresh status. The test explicitly proves a fresh recovery after both the requester grant and original intent windows have elapsed.

A real recipient would have to authenticate and durably retain preparation before sending. The inert gate names that as an explicit local precondition. Its boolean collaborators do not prove decryption or disk persistence. Separately, a deterministic carried-worker ML-KEM/AEAD fixture is actually decrypted and authenticated natively, and a changed tag is actually rejected. The authority cannot infer successful recipient decryption merely from the sender's valid signature. The permission projection does not create an acknowledgement, activate a session root, insert an application entry or securely erase anything.

Complete authenticated histories must extend retained history. A valid same-origin fork fences the recipient and replay cannot heal it. During new-reference review I noticed that an exact replay inside a supplied history could leave the ledger sequence unchanged while consuming another supplied row; the fold now checks every row against its one-based resulting sequence, and duplicate-history refusal is in the corpus. The first fixture-generation attempt also stopped because the inherited in-memory active-device set was not JSON serializable. It now publishes a sorted list of the exact same identifiers. That failed generation was before any conformance assertion and is retained as a failure rather than counted as a passing run. Neither repair changed predecessor protocol or laboratory source.

The existing rev0027 binding lane passed 152 checks before integration. The expanded new direct corpus passed 251 checks after the exact dependency-only refresh. That is source-scope evidence, not advance knowledge of the final HTML. The completed-carrier matrix, compiler reproduction and archive custody must be read in the appended rev0028 release closure. Prior histories are deep-copied; no current packaging, compiler or finding update may alter a preserved historical object. The workshop adds intents, a separate intent lane, exact source reading/export and impact coverage; comparison can inspect rev0002 through rev0028 without executing an older carrier.

This turn opened four primary HTML sources, recorded as T149–T152. They informed the distinctions between freshness and decisions, identical effects and exact saved responses, revocation and propagation, and single-authority atomicity versus two-store transactions. They do not confer RFC conformance or an independent audit. All earlier provider options and dated reviews remain intact. No account, provider change, live service, deployment or dependency fetch was performed.

My recommendation is a creation-only private single-writer authority adapter, still separate from recipients and product chat. It must co-commit the frozen cutover and the Intentglass event under the same original authority lock and transaction. A second independently committed or asynchronously mirrored journal is not equivalent. Prove exact interrupted-send recovery, commit/abort races, crash/restart, older restore and divergent authenticated history before a recipient adapter consumes these decisions. Multiple selected origins, recipient key revocation/replacement, independent endpoint roles and chat integration remain separately scoped work. We do not gain a live service by renaming a memory-only reference. Preserve the exact donors, old letters, constitution, and honest distinctions between pass, fail and unavailable.

### 156.9 Ordered work for the next officer

Start by inspecting this exact carrier and its inert `intents --full` record. Do not infer a runtime Intentglass origin from any public deterministic fixture. ### 157.7 Canonical bytes, release custody and handoff boundary

Here, an exact request identity and retained result refer to the strict admitted canonical record and its signed fields. Harmless raw-JSON whitespace is not a second cryptographic operation. Decoded duplicate keys, fractional/exponent forms, negative zero, unsafe integers, malformed UTF-8, surrogates, trailing values and oversized input are refused by the raw admission boundary. A changed signed field, nonce, coordinate, signature or operation does not borrow a saved decision. Exact-result recovery returns the originally retained canonical result bytes; it does not re-sign an equivalent newly timed object.

Release custody closes outside the three-file archive after this document's final bytes are fixed. Its checks require exactly three unique regular root members named `Vibechat.html`, `BOOTSTRAPROSE.md` and `test.sh`; no directory entries, extra files, private runtime state or external receipts belong in the ZIP. The completed ZIP must pass its CRC test, be independently extracted to a new absent directory, and have all three extracted members compared byte-for-byte and by SHA-256 with the fixed release inputs. The independently extracted HTML must pass its carried manifest verification and inert Intentglass source-binding summary, and the extracted development driver must equal its carried source. The final handoff reports the completed results, not an assumed future outcome.

The ZIP hash and this bootstrap's final hash belong in the external custody receipt, not recursively inside this document. No self-hash or final archive hash is guessed. The fixed tested HTML hash above is safe to retain here because this markdown is outside that HTML. Closing the markdown and checking the archive must not trigger another HTML reseal; any subsequent HTML edit requires a fresh applicable final-carrier test run.

**Next gate remains creation-only private durable authority ordering.** Co-commit the exact frozen requester cutover and the matching Intentglass event under the same original authority lock and transaction; do not substitute an asynchronously mirrored second ledger. Prove interrupted sends, exact saved responses, both commit/abort and commit/cutover winners, crash/restart and retained-knowledge rollback/fork behavior before a recipient adapter consumes decisions. A later recipient adapter must separately prove authentication and preparation persistence before intent release, local atomic settlement after the exact authority decision, and honest abandonment/recovery semantics. Recipient key revocation/replacement, independent endpoint roles, general activation and product browser/CLI integration remain separate gates.

The new authority uses the same original `order` subdirectory and original lock/database/key/anchor/capability paths. It adds `intent_origin` and `intent_events` tables to that database only during new fixture creation. The encrypted origin row is bound to the complete selected admission, frozen signed session, exact prepared settlement, requester trust and recipient authorization. Each intent row retains the signed history entry and exact canonical event response under the existing authenticated row encryption scheme.

The original `requests`, `events` and `meta` structures continue to hold frozen Orderglass order and exact responses. Their new creation-only schema marker prevents an old opener from accepting a directory which requires Intentglass enforcement. The origin and selection-bundle identities are retained in authority metadata and checked against the private creation bundle. This bundle is not a private key export and is not a reusable production origin.

The participant's existing prepared snapshot is marked archive-only. It still records authenticated preparation, not successful application admission. No active session root, consumed tombstone, application entry or acknowledgement is created by the new authority adapter. A new future participant gate must make its own explicit transition from an exact retained preparation; merely opening the current archive with an old command is refused.

Creation initially owns the absent tree through the delegated creator. Only after successful ownership acquisition may later failure remove that tree. The reviewed synthetic losing-creator case writes a competing sentinel and raises before ownership; the sentinel survives. Existing and symlink destinations refuse without adoption. This is an explicit bounded cleanup test, not a general proof against a hostile process with the same filesystem credentials.

### 158.3 The transaction seam

For a new terminal decision the authority begins one immediate transaction, validates the pinned origin and retained history, derives the exact reference event, signs it, retains the encrypted event and exact response, updates its monotonic floor and commits. It then publishes the signed local combined anchor and returns the retained canonical event. An existing matching terminal decision is validated as exact replay and read from its stored bytes; no signature is regenerated.

For a requester cutover the adapter uses the original frozen validation and record construction, but replaces the commit seam so that frozen event insertion, frozen request/response retention, original metadata update, matching Intentglass event insertion and exact event-response retention share one transaction. The inherited independently committing method is not called as a precursor to a second intent commit. Both projections are folded and checked when the database opens.

The ten named abrupt-exit boundaries are carried in the memorandum and exposed only through the explicit laboratory serve crash option:

```text
before-decision-transaction
after-decision-insert
before-decision-commit
after-decision-commit-before-anchor
after-decision-anchor-before-response
after-frozen-cutover-insert
after-cutover-intent-insert
before-cutover-commit
after-cutover-commit-before-anchor
after-cutover-anchor-before-response
```

The corpus executes five commit edges, five cutover edges and two abort edges, for twelve actual authority exits. Exact-client retry is a separate explicit action. The corpus also injects an actual SQL abort between cutover halves and an anchor-publication exception after commit. These are process and software exception controls, not simulated claims of hardware failure.

### 158.4 One local anchor and its limit

The combined history begins with the selected admission operation. Subsequent items are consecutive Intentglass event identities, including the event which binds the frozen cutover. The anchor contains the selected origin, creation bundle digest, original database/fixture/authority identities, combined sequence/head/history digest and separate frozen-order and intent prefixes. It is written under the same original writer lock after the database transaction.

A crash may leave the database ahead of that anchor. On restart a complete authenticated descendant permits catch-up; it does not permit changing a terminal response. An anchor ahead of a restored older database refuses. At equal length, a conflicting authenticated head/history refuses. Restoring every local observation to an earlier consistent state remains indistinguishable; the local authority cannot claim an external observation it does not possess.

The restore corpus copies deliberately closed private test trees. It is not an operational recipe for copying only a live SQLite main file, and it does not qualify storage hardware or uncooperative access. File permissions, advisory locking and authenticated encryption name different boundaries. None alone proves a globally current history.

### 158.5 Lost replies, unverified replies and retained decisions

The frozen Orderglass response format is not a general parser for the new bare signed terminal event. Reusing it would either reject valid new responses or weaken a predecessor contract. Decisionglass therefore carries a separate bounded client which validates canonical response bytes, exact selected intent/session/preparation binding, authority signatures and the frozen reference's terminal semantics. It never treats the transport capability as sufficient identity authorization.

A review of the first sealed candidate found that a non-200 response was recorded as refusal and a failed success verifier could leave the send journal at preparation. A request may already have executed before either reply problem. The hardened client records post-send uncertainty for both conditions and does not publish a successful response file. Its bounded diagnostic can explain an HTTP status or code but cannot confer nonexecution, successful cancellation or permission to issue new work.

Two additional private separate-process tests substitute the reply after a real authority commit and anchor publication. One sends an unsigned HTTP error; the other changes the actual returned event signature without changing its selected body. Both cause client exit 75 and an uncertainty entry. The authority is then closed and reopened, its committed terminal decision is verified, and a healthy exact retry returns the original retained event without appending another transition. These tests are controlled collaborators in the corpus, not new public fault endpoints.

The client may separately request a fresh signed read proof for exact recovery. It does not renew an expired intent or grant. A recovery result is the original signed event, not a claim of present authorization or new permission. A negative or missing reply is not a signed terminal abort. Conversely, a known complete authority commit still does not reconstruct missing local preparation or create a recipient database transaction.

### 158.6 An explicit manual exercise

The automatic `decisionlab` lane is the reproducible exercise. The following manual workflow performs one additional synthetic commit and recovery. Use a local private scratch directory, not a shared filesystem or a production profile. The fixture has short new-work lifetimes; the commands intentionally construct the request shortly before sending rather than leaving an old request to be silently renewed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
umask 077
HTML="$(realpath Vibechat.html)"
BASE="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/decisionglass.XXXXXXXX")"
ROOT="$BASE/fixture"                         # This child must be absent.

bash "$HTML" decision-lab-new --directory "$ROOT"
bash "$HTML" decision-lab-serve --directory "$ROOT" --port 0 \
  --ready-file "$BASE/ready.json" >"$BASE/authority.log" 2>&1 &
AUTHORITY_PID=$!
trap 'kill "$AUTHORITY_PID" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$AUTHORITY_PID" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT

# Bounded readiness wait; it neither installs dependencies nor starts another service.
for _ in $(seq 1 200); do
  test -s "$BASE/ready.json" && break
  kill -0 "$AUTHORITY_PID"
  sleep 0.1
done
test -s "$BASE/ready.json"
URL="$(python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))["url"])' "$BASE/ready.json")"

bash "$HTML" decision-lab-request --directory "$ROOT" --kind commit \
  --output "$BASE/commit-request.json"
bash "$HTML" decision-lab-send --directory "$ROOT" --url "$URL" \
  --request "$BASE/commit-request.json" --output "$BASE/decision.json"
bash "$HTML" decision-lab-request --directory "$ROOT" --kind recover \
  --output "$BASE/recover-request.json"
bash "$HTML" decision-lab-send --directory "$ROOT" --url "$URL" \
  --request "$BASE/recover-request.json" --output "$BASE/recovered.json"
cmp "$BASE/decision.json" "$BASE/recovered.json"

kill "$AUTHORITY_PID"
wait "$AUTHORITY_PID"
trap - EXIT
bash "$HTML" decision-lab-inspect --directory "$ROOT"
```

The printed URL contains only loopback host, port and route; the capability is read from its private file by the explicit client. Request and response outputs are private, absent-destination files. The inspector uses the authority writer lock, so close the server before inspecting rather than opening a concurrent database connection. The scratch tree contains co-located synthetic secrets and must never be added to the release archive.

For an exact retry after uncertainty, preserve the original request file and choose a new absent response destination. Do not rebuild the request with a new operation, manually edit its timestamp or interpret a failed output-file write as absence of the authority decision. `decision-lab-request --kind abort` and `--kind cutover` are explicit separate actions for a fresh test selection; the six-order corpus demonstrates their precedence. An already committed intent cannot be successfully aborted. Creating a new unrelated laboratory after expiry is not recovery of the prior selection.

### 158.8 Research completed this turn

Four official HTML sources were opened and read on 2026-10-06. The following T153–T156 records are also carried in `research.json`. They inform the specific implementation choices, not an RFC-conformance badge or independent review. All earlier technical-source entries, 37 infrastructure candidates and their actual dated review scopes are retained. No provider entry was merely stamped current without being reviewed.


**T153 — SQLite — Write-Ahead Logging, one writer and the current WAL-reset advisory**  
Source: https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html  
Checked: 2026-10-06. WAL coordinates writers locally and commits within one database, not across independent stores. The current WAL-reset advisory names the fix in 3.51.3 and later, with 3.44.6 and 3.50.7 backports. This environment reports 3.46.1; no engine upgrade is claimed. Decisionglass uses one cooperating connection under the original flock, rather than concurrent independent write/checkpoint connections. A maintained fixed engine remains a deployment prerequisite; this is not vulnerability reproduction or hardware qualification.

**T154 — SQLite — PRAGMA synchronous, verified FULL policy and storage assumptions**  
Source: https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_synchronous  
Checked: 2026-10-06. SQLite documents FULL as value 2 and describes its additional WAL synchronization before transaction completion. Decisionglass inherits and verifies WAL/FULL on the original connection. Process-exit and SQL-exception tests exercise application ordering, not physical power-loss or storage-hardware guarantees. The setting is not an independent audit or evidence that a recipient database also committed.

**T155 — SQLite — Corruption prevention, consistent backup and coordinated access**  
Source: https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html  
Checked: 2026-10-06. SQLite warns against inconsistent live file copies, losing recovery journals and incompatible locking disciplines, and identifies consistent backup approaches. Decisionglass restore/fork fixtures copy closed test trees rather than advocating live raw-file backup. A surviving local anchor can detect a different authenticated history, not repair corrupted storage or detect joint rollback of every observation. The advisory flock only coordinates cooperating processes.

**T156 — RFC 9110 §9.2.2 — Repeated effects, uncertain replies and explicit exact recovery**  
Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2  
Checked: 2026-10-06. HTTP idempotency concerns intended effects; a repeated response may differ. Non-idempotent requests are not generally safe to retry without known application semantics. Decisionglass makes a stronger, separately tested application promise: retain original decision bytes and explicitly retry the identical signed request or use a fresh bounded read proof. A missing reply is uncertain, never evidence of successful abort, nonexecution or permission to invent a new operation.

### 158.9 New constitutional articles

Earlier articles remain exact; these are appended rather than used to rewrite history.

**C83 — A cutover has one durable authority transaction, not two successful mirrors**

A Decisionglass frozen requester cutover, matching Intentglass event and their exact saved responses SHALL be co-committed under the original Orderglass writer lock, connection and SQLite transaction. Committing two individually valid journals in succession does not implement one order. An opener SHALL refuse orphan halves, mismatched selection, nonconsecutive history, or authenticated divergence from retained knowledge. The combined signed local anchor may catch up only along an authenticated descendant; it is not an independent witness or a cross-store transaction.

**C84 — Creation ownership and old-opener fencing are explicit boundaries**

The Decisionglass adapter SHALL activate only while constructing a new absent private synthetic fixture. It SHALL NOT adopt an existing authority or infer activation from an old signed head. The creation preparation is an archive, fenced from a predecessor participant opener; its existence is not a recipient integration. A creator SHALL NOT remove a path which it failed to acquire, including a concurrent winning creator. Synthetic co-located endpoint and authority keys do not establish endpoint isolation. Private filesystem capabilities gate transport but do not replace record-level identity authorization.

**C85 — A storage error requires reopen; a missing response is not an abort**

A storage or anchor-publication error after mutation SHALL invalidate the Decisionglass handle; only reopening and validating durable state may determine whether the exact decision committed. A prewrite semantic refusal may roll back without poisoning a healthy service. Lost replies, unsigned post-send HTTP errors and invalid success responses SHALL remain uncertain, not be recast as successful abort or nonexecution; explicit retry uses the identical retained request and operation, or a separately authorized exact-result read. Recovery returns the original saved signature bytes and does not renew permission. Abrupt process exits and injected SQL errors are not physical power-loss certification, and an authority decision is not recipient application persistence or acknowledgement.

**letter-0033-officer · 2026-10-06 · Vibechat rev0029 Decisionglass continuation officer (assistant)**

To the next sandperson: the owner again asked us to run the bootstrap and continue. The received rev0028 Intentglass trio is the parent. I chose its recommended next gate: a creation-only private durable authority adapter. Decisionglass preserves the frozen authority-decision-first/exact-settlement/v1 policy and all predecessor implementation bytes. It does not wire product chat, turn an existing authority into a new service, isolate endpoint keys or make an application entry.

The critical seam is the original Orderglass transaction. A frozen cutover and a matching Intentglass event cannot be independently committed and then described as one order. The adapter holds the original flock, uses the original SQLite connection and database, inserts both signed records and encrypted exact response bytes, updates the original metadata and commits once. Terminal commit and abort decisions use the same writer. The original admission remains the creation prefix. The combined local signed anchor authenticates this bounded order and separately binds both frozen and new coordinates.

Creation deliberately runs locally without listeners: real synthetic Loopglass reservation, real Orderglass admission, and actual carried session payload authentication followed by retained preparation. The same process holds both synthetic endpoint roles; the fixture keys and authority keys are co-located private material. After preparation, the participant metadata becomes archive-only so an older Passageglass command cannot bypass the new gate. The authority has a new creation-only schema and origin, and old Orderglass/Sightglass openers refuse it. A populated existing authority is never migrated. The only subsequent listener is an explicitly requested capability-gated loopback authority; a separate synthetic request client signs and retains its exact intent before sending.

Commit-first still authorizes only the selected prepared settlement to finish later. Abort-first or cutover-first blocks undecided work. Abort after a committed decision is too late. The authority does not recycle a reservation, create another admission or contact Loopglass at decision time. Each terminal event is encrypted and retained with exact response bytes. Exact replay uses those bytes, not a newly generated signature. A separately recipient-signed fresh bounded read proof recovers a terminal result after the original grant and request windows. Missing replies are uncertain; a client records uncertainty and an explicit exact retry, never a guessed abort or a new nonce.

The direct corpus exercises all six event orderings, actual HTTP refusals, and twelve abrupt process exits at ten named edges. Those edges include inserting only the frozen cutover, inserting its Intentglass companion, immediately before COMMIT, after COMMIT but before anchor publication, and after anchor publication before response. Restart sees both cutover halves or neither. A real SQLite trigger abort after the first insertion proves rollback of that half; an injected postcommit anchor-write error proves that failure cannot turn into an apparent success or a second in-memory decision. Mutating storage failures poison the handle and require reopen. Ordinary prewrite semantic refusals leave a usable service after rollback.

A surviving later combined anchor detects an older restored database or an equal-length same-key divergent terminal history. A lagging anchor can catch up only to an authenticated descendant. A deliberate joint rollback of every local observation remains accepted as indistinguishable locally; this is the named limit, not a missing test to hide. The authority signature never proves recipient decryption or local application persistence. A future recipient adapter must enforce those local prerequisites and its own atomic commit.

Review caught a cleanup ownership error before the release: a creator which lost the absent-directory race must not delete the winner. Cleanup now requires ownership established after successful delegated creation; the corpus has a synthetic concurrent-creation collaborator and checks preservation. Inspection also showed that the original Orderglass client accepts only its frozen wrapper response; it cannot honestly stand in for a bare Intentglass event. The new client has its own bounded transport and signature/binding validation rather than relaxing the predecessor response contract. The first direct corpus stopped on a test expectation spelling: the frozen refusal is coordinates-binding, not coordinate-binding. The expectation was corrected without changing the refusal. A workshop assembly helper also stopped before producing a carrier because it matched a script token inside the loader rather than an actual anchored source block; only the helper's boundary selection was corrected.

After the first sealed candidate, response review found that post-send HTTP errors and unverified success bodies must not be journaled as refusal or nonexecution. The first candidate run was deliberately interrupted after CLI and transport passed. The client now retains uncertainty for every post-send failure and returns exit 75; two additional actual authority/client response collaborators substitute an unsigned error or an invalid signature AFTER the authority commits. Reopen proves the decision exists and healthy exact retry retrieves it without another event. These twelve checks expanded the repaired direct source run to 238 scoped checks. That is not advance knowledge of the finished HTML. Exact final-carrier lane results, reproduction and archive custody are in bootstrap section 159. All old records are deep-copied rather than sharing mutable release metadata. Source-binding refresh updates dependency digests, not frozen vectors, signatures or wire formats. The workshop adds decisionlab and five explicit runtime commands, three named source members, a twenty-seventh lane and source-impact/compare coverage.

This turn read four official HTML sources, recorded as T153–T156: SQLite WAL, synchronous policy, corruption-prevention/backup guidance, and RFC 9110 retry semantics. SQLite's current WAL-reset advisory is material: the runtime here reports 3.46.1, not a fixed engine. The adapter retains one cooperating connection under the original flock, and tests do not model uncooperative external tools or qualify hardware persistence. Future deployment should use a maintained fixed engine. No vulnerability reproducer, engine upgrade, dependency fetch, provider account, public listener or publication is part of this turn.

Recommend the next gate as a creation-only recipient adapter using this exact durable authority decision. Retain authenticated preparation before releasing the intent; consume only a complete matching committed event; atomically persist the application entry, active root, consumed local prekey tombstone and exact binding; then retain acknowledgement. Prove missing preparation, local abandonment, terminal abort, commit-first/later-cutover, lost response, crash/restart and postcommit acknowledgement order. Keep endpoint isolation and chat integration separate until that seam is demonstrated.
